Had they remained at the DOJ into January 2027, they would have spent the year under oath at a witness table, answering Democratic subpoenas about political prosecutions, dismantled enforcement units, and discarded desegregation decrees. Nevertheless, these lawyers aren’t abandoning their crusade against multiracial democracy. Instead, they’re trading in their government paychecks for conservative dark-money funding and resuming the fight.

Take Dhillon, who is heading straight back into private practice. Long before Trump nominated her to run the Civil Rights Division, Dhillon built a high-profile career at the Dhillon Law Group and her nonprofit litigation outfit, the Center for American Liberty, perfecting the core business model of the modern conservative legal movement (and funneling nonprofit donations to her private firm in the process). That model doesn’t require an office at DOJ. In the current environment, it only requires manufacturing ideological grievances, packaging them as novel constitutional injuries, and routing them through handpicked federal district and appellate judges straight to a six-justice conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court.

During the first Trump administration and the Biden years, Dhillon reliably produced impact litigation founded in conservative cultural grievance. She represented former Google engineer James Damore in a class-action suit claiming Silicon Valley discriminated against white conservative men. She launched high-profile lawsuits targeting gender-affirming medical care and school trans-inclusion policies. When state and local governments enacted emergency public health measures during the Covid-19 pandemic, Dhillon’s group secured shadow docket victories from the Supreme Court that rewrote First Amendment doctrine on the fly and subordinated public health to religious exemptions. And when Trump tried to overturn the 2020 election, Dhillon was right there advising the campaign, openly banking on Trump-appointed justices like Amy Coney Barrett to step in and deliver the presidency.

Getting a primo posting at the DOJ was an opportunity for Dhillion to take her show directly to the halls of power, but it certainly wasn’t necessary for her main goal of teeing up cases for our conservative overlords on the Supreme Court. If anything, the 19-month wrecking ball of Trump DOJ leadership cleared away some of the institutional obstacles standing in her path, leaving fewer defenses against the private lawsuits her firm traditionally levies.

By the time Dhillon stepped down, more than 75 percent of the Civil Rights Division’s career staff had been driven out. Consider what that wreckage means the moment Dhillon and her peers walk back into private practice. Historically, when conservative litigants went to federal court to gut the Voting Rights Act, roll back workplace antidiscrimination rules, or challenge civil rights protections, the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division brought its institutional expertise, statutory authority, and decades of enforcement data to defend federal civil rights laws. By hollowing out that division from the inside, Dhillon and her colleagues kneecapped the federal government’s primary civil rights watchdog. When private, conservative firms file their next wave of lawsuits attacking voting access, public school equity policies, or corporate diversity programs, the DOJ won’t be in their way.

And the judges waiting to hear those cases haven’t gone anywhere. The Supreme Court’s conservative majority is openly inviting private litigators to keep feeding its docket. Seemingly based on the fact that Black students are still being accepted at prestigious universities after the court outlawed race-conscious admissions, Justice Samuel Alito warned conservative activists that “diligent judicial enforcement … will be needed going forward” to counteract universities’ “considerable resistance” to the court’s 2023 decision in Students for Fair Admissions. Alito’s pointed echoing of liberal criticism of white Southern politicians’ “massive resistance” to Brown v. Board of Education was certainly not lost on a room full of conservatives with persecution complexes. Even as Black enrollment at elite universities has plummeted to its lowest levels in decades, white conservatives somehow remain the real oppressed minority group in the United States. Because federal judges can’t file lawsuits themselves, a sitting justice calling for “diligent judicial enforcement” at a conservative gala is an unmistakable signal to private lawyers like Dhillon to keep bringing the cases so the court can finish the job.

Congressional committees can haul former DOJ officials before cameras to build a public record of how the department was abused, but they can’t strip life tenure from the hundreds of right-wing judges Trump installed across the federal bench, or alter the math on a Supreme Court that has spent the past several years dismantling the administrative state, inventing new constitutional shields for corporate and religious plaintiffs, and reserving final policymaking authority for itself.

The conservative legal movement understood decades ago that controlling the judiciary is far more durable than winning any single election. As long as the Roberts court remains intact in its current form, right-wing lawyers do not need a badge from the Justice Department to strip workers, voters, and marginalized communities of their rights. They just need a willing plaintiff and a sympathetic bench.

Celebrating the exit of Harmeet Dhillon and her colleagues mistakes a tactical retreat for a structural victory. These lawyers didn’t need DOJ titles to dismantle civil rights protections, kneecap federal agencies, or rewrite constitutional doctrine before they entered government, and they won’t need them now that they are heading back into private practice, so long as a six-justice conservative supermajority on pace to hold power for decades sits waiting to capitalize on their next wave of grievance litigation. The pipeline isn’t going anywhere, so Democrats need to look beyond oversight hearings and confront the institution that makes the conservative legal movement’s business model effective.

The new Congress needs to expand the Supreme Court to break its entrenched right-wing majority while considering its constitutional authority to strip the court of jurisdiction over core civil rights laws, channel litigation away from handpicked conservative judges, require a supermajority of justices to strike down federal statutes, and establish fast-track congressional review to override activist rulings. Until Democrats both rebalance the bench and strip it of the unchecked power it has hoarded for itself, these resignations won’t protect a single person—they’ll just move the battlefield back to where conservatives already own the judges.

items.title: Inside the American Girl Empire
items.content_text:
For many Americans, the fortieth anniversary of American Girl hits core memories harder than the 250th anniversary of the country itself. Abraham Lincoln supposedly read Parson Weems’s biography of George Washington in a log cabin by candlelight. Many more read American Girl books by flashlight on carpeted floors and in canopy beds, on road trips and in tree houses, at home with parents and in public libraries with friends. The dolls and their books didn’t just teach history; they were history.

In 1986, educator and entrepreneur Pleasant Rowland launched a doll company and soon released a set of three fictional historical figures. Kirsten Larson was a blond-ringleted, Swedish immigrant whose family settled the 1854 Minnesota frontier. Samantha Parkington was a dark-haired, orphaned rich girl raised by her grandmother in 1904 New York. Molly McIntire was the bespectacled girl with mousy brown braids swinging behind her on the World War II home front in 1944 Illinois.

According to legend, Rowland had the idea while looking up at interwoven tree branches on a trip to Colonial Williamsburg in the early 1980s, not unlike Isaac Newton theorizing about gravity under an apple tree: She would teach history and instill values through 18-inch-tall, historically themed dolls. Toy industry executives doubted her vision for combining publishing, toys, direct mail, and clothing in one company. They were wrong. The brand proved iconic, and in 1998, she sold Pleasant Company to Mattel for $700 million.

Money can measure value, but so can the meaningful conversations that pour out of hundreds of thousands of women who grew up with American Girl. If you talk to any woman under the age of 50, she will likely tell you what a doll has taught her about American history and what that experience meant to her. Even the many who could not afford the dolls—priced between $68 and $95 in 1986—likely have strong opinions about the brand.

Forty years in, two new books offer competing histories of the company that shaped a generation’s sense of the past and our understanding of ourselves. One is a business history of American Girl from 1986 to the present, An American Girl: How a Billion-Dollar Doll and Its Unlikely Founder Changed Girlhood Forever by journalist Amanda FitzSimons, published by Atria. The other is a history of Pleasant Company from 1986 to 1998, The Making of American Girl: The history of the brand’s creative journey told through photos, sketches, swatches, artifacts, and early designs from the American Girl Archives, whose author is identified only as American Girl Publishing.

The corporate-written history tells a quintessentially American story: the ascent of Pleasant Company. Through products that offered a window into a whole world, American Girl created new and empowering experiences for American girls who were old enough to read and young enough to crave role models who were kids like them. Yet Amanda FitzSimons’s often critical book may make a more convincing case for the importance of American Girl, showing how it reached its young customers’ deepest needs: not only to collect but also to connect, to belong, and to aspire.


The Making of American Girl is big. Seriously, it’s huge. My copy broke the American Girl–branded bag handed to me by a smiling cashier. Its size allows the book to include, as the subtitle lists, “photos, sketches, swatches, artifacts, and early designs,” as well as 282 pages of text. Each of the original six dolls—Samantha Parkington (representing 1904, released in 1986), Kirsten Larson (representing 1854, released in 1986), Molly McIntire (representing 1944, released in 1986), Felicity Merriman (representing 1774, released in 1991), Addy Walker (representing 1864, released in 1993), and Josefina Montoya (representing 1824, released in 1998)—has a full two-page portrait, reminiscent of the original mail-order catalogs. The colors are vibrant, literally including swatches from each doll’s color palette. The carefully curated images douse the reader in nostalgia.

If you talk to any woman under the age of 50, she will likely tell you what a doll has taught her about American history and what that experience meant to her.

We begin at the start not of American history but, rather, of American Girl. Around Christmas 1983, Rowland sat in her family’s cottage in rural Wisconsin and scribbled a business plan: for characters, products, a magazine, and eventually, a store “that would have historical displays like little museums.” Originally, she chose periods around a half-century apart, conveying the scaffolding of American history as her education taught her to imagine it: a European immigrant in the mid-nineteenth century, a girl from the Progressive era, and a girl from World War II. The book describes the first six dolls’ lore and associated merchandise in loving detail. Felicity, for instance, proudly wears pants and stands next to a horse in the center of a page. According to canon, both the pants and the horse are stolen, from her father’s apprentice and the local tanner, respectively. She “borrowed” the pants to rebel against traditional gender norms and “freed” the horse from abuse, promptly naming her Independence, or Penny for short.

From 1986 to 1998, Pleasant Company dolls and accessories were only available through the mail-order catalog. This was by design: “You’d never see a stack of Molly dolls, God forbid, jammed into a grocery store-style shelf at Toys ‘R’ Us with her wire-rimmed glasses haphazardly askew,” FitzSimons writes. They were scarce and therefore more precious, more like artifacts than ordinary toys. The catalog itself was a treasure, which could be obtained by mailing a postcard from the back of an American Girl book to Pleasant Company. In my own research, I chatted with an archivist who decades ago could not afford the products and had no clue how the catalog reached her rural home, yet she read it like a favorite story. For the Christmas season in 1986, Pleasant Company distributed 500,000 catalogs with a revenue goal of $1 million, and by the end of the calendar year, almost doubled the goal by reaching $1.8 million.

The Making of American Girl repeatedly addresses criticism, starting small and probing deeper. Samantha Parkington was marketed as “Victorian,” when she represented 1904, which was technically the Edwardian period. The book implies that the company wanted to capture a mood rather than a precise historical period: Valerie Tripp, the author of many titles in the American Girl series, remembers “sitting with Pleasant and a historian consultant who was waxing on about the Victorian/Edwardian period and describing what he thought Samantha should be like, which to my mind sounded passive, clichéd, and utterly humorless.… Pleasant … kicked me under the table—and I knew that kick meant, ‘VT, this is exactly what we do NOT want Samantha to be.’” Rowland and Tripp were less interested in correct terminology than in building a world that felt like magic to consumers.

The Kirsten section includes two full pages on Singing Bird, her underdeveloped Dakota friend from the 1986 book Kirsten Learns a Lesson, and it explains the company’s subsequent efforts to do better (though it did not collaborate with Dakota experts to publish a revised version until 2025). The second page of the section on Felicity, the American Revolution doll, is titled “The Question of Freedom,” and displays framed images of the enslaved characters Rose and Marcus, along with a picture of Felicity’s free Black friend, Isaac—as if responding to media scholar Emilie Zaslow’s claim that the Black characters in Felicity’s stories are “nameless, faceless, and voiceless.” Yet, although Felicity’s stories take place in Williamsburg from 1774 to 1776, no Black characters flee to join the British, as thousands did in real life. That would disrupt Pleasant Company’s framing of the question of freedom, which centered the patriots’ revolution as a war for liberation for all.


The omniscient author of The Making of American Girl might not like Amanda FitzSimons. The Making of American Girl and An American Girl differ in that the former presents the history of a business, while An American Girl analyzes history through a business lens: How did Rowland’s luxury goods—aimed at such a specific stage of childhood for education and play—attract and retain such massive consumer demand? What broader cultural forces—such as gender, race, class, and their intersections—enabled the success of Rowland’s empire? These questions are at the heart of FitzSimons’s page-turner, in which she recalls that she felt safe when she flew as an unaccompanied minor in the early 1990s—she had Molly McIntire in tow. So, really, she was in good company.

She first learned about the woman behind the dolls while on assignment for Bustle in 2022, reporting on a small New York town where Rowland purchased over 15 buildings—which is its own wild story about who controls historical preservation. This more recent escapade led FitzSimons to research Rowland’s better-known life’s work. In her account, Rowland is captivating: an educator both idealistic and savvy, and an entrepreneur both creative and cushioned by privilege. In 1986, Rowland had a million dollars from the sale of Superkids, a reading program she had launched in 1978, padded by at least an additional million from her husband, to launch her toy company independently.

While formal education and historic sites have typically focused on the actions of great men, Rowland invited girls to imagine what the American Revolution or another historical event was like for kids just like them.

But the business history of American Girl is not a one-woman story. It’s a million-girl success, and FitzSimons pays good attention to the hordes of consumers. “When you spend several years telling people that you’re writing a book about American Girl,” she writes, “you find yourself on the receiving end of teary-eyed memories, minor customer service complaints and monologues typically reserved for the last five minutes of therapy.” Pleasant Company helped girls understand themselves as part of history. While formal education and historic sites have typically focused on the actions of great men, Rowland invited girls to imagine what the American Revolution or another historical event was like for kids just like them. The franchise combined more typical doll play with the intellectual adventure of exploring and claiming a part in history.

Pleasant Company curated strong female role models from an imaginary past. The accessories or artifacts; the details, including pet names; and the well-developed story arcs made historical fiction characters feel real. Customers collected the protagonists and material culture of the American Girl universe, while also seeking connection with family and friends and a sense of belonging in history and in the world around them. Struggles to find belonging at school or in a misogynistic culture increased the appeal of an imagined past.

In 1991, Pleasant Company introduced a new doll for the first time since the original three. Felicity’s debut took place at Colonial Williamsburg with an Elegant Tea Party that attracted 11,000 guests, and it lasted over eight days with 24 seatings. FitzSimons describes the atmosphere as “a mash-up of a nineties wedding of a very fancy cousin, a Daughters of the American Revolution convention, and lunchtime in the dining hall of a posh all-girls boarding school.”

FitzSimons implies that the tea party also amplified a demand among fans for greater diversity in American Girl’s offerings. The event showed how white the company and its products were, she writes, quoting an attendee who told The Washington Post at the time that she “looked around and saw only white girls wearing expensive dresses.” Two years later, in 1993, Pleasant Company introduced the first Black American Girl doll, Addy Walker. The Making of American Girl says that including “a Civil War–era Black character” among the dolls was always part of the vision, going back to 1984, though FitzSimons suggests fans helped drive the new release.

FitzSimons also notes that in early 1993, Oprah Winfrey remarked that all American Girl dolls were white, and in late 1993, her on-air endorsement of Addy crashed the Pleasant Company phone lines. Why wouldn’t The Making of American Girl include that detail? American Girl Publishing is not afraid to toot its own horn, but the story it tells is of the vision of a founding figure: “In the pages of this book, you’ll read the story of how Pleasant Rowland created a collection of magical moments for girls.” In this telling, the dolls aren’t supposed to be seen as products shaped by marketing, supply, and demand.

The 1998 opening of American Girl Place in Chicago marked the first time that American Girl products were available for in-person purchase. Nonetheless, it was supposed to feel more like a museum or gallery than a shop. The in-person shops in Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, Nashville, New York City, Orlando, and Washington, D.C., are each called an American Girl Place, never a “store.” The dolls on display with their accessories are set up like exhibits, not on sales racks, even though all products are available for purchase.


Felicity’s $110 canopy bed costs $110 more than the uncomfortable Murphy bed that came attached to the wall in my current abode. My thirteenth-floor, 325-square-foot apartment houses so many American Girls that some friends call it the Dollhouse in the Sky. What prevents me from selling my six 18-inch dolls if they could pay a month or two of rent? Why endure the hassle of bring them with me on move after move? Why would a materially insecure adult need luxury items from childhood?

It takes both The Making of American Girl and An American Girl to answer my question. The official narrative underscores the original vision for the dolls, while FitzSimons explains how they captured a generation’s psyche. The dolls are protagonists of sacred texts, representations of a past but still present part of myself, and proof that history came alive.

items.title: Trump Dedicates Entire Speech to Ripping Into His First 2028 Target
items.content_text:
Election Day 2026 proved that the American public is tired of high gas prices, impossible affordability levels, and the Iran war. But rather than meaningfully address any of that, the president has decided to turn his gaze toward Gavin Newsom.

Donald Trump addressed the Justice Department Monday in a speech that almost singularly focused on the California governor and his recent decision to spare all of California’s death row inmates—some 548 of them. Pending the approval of the state Supreme Court for a few cases, those prisoners will now serve life in prison instead of facing the death penalty.

“Gavin Newsom coddles murderers, rapists, and other scum of the Earth criminals because he is devoid of a soul ... unable to comprehend the hurt he is causing victims’ families and loved ones,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote on X prior to Trump’s speech. “God will not judge him well.”

Newsom is widely expected to throw his hat in the ring for the 2028 presidential race, and will reportedly reveal his plan as soon as early January. He is one of the few national Democratic standouts who has heavily hinted at a potential bid for the Democratic nomination, aside from former Vice President Kamala Harris.

But Trump is, nonetheless, opting to give Newsom more attention.

“Governor Newsom is failing the victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these barbaric child killers and serial killers. These murderers raped, tortured and terrorized innocent victims. Governor Newsom must stop playing politics with public safety,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

The White House has singled out 20 convicted killers from Newsom’s clemency proposal, highlighting the various crimes they’ve committed, including murdering children, sexual abuse, torture, and serial murder. But Newsom has defended his decision against capital punishment.

“California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that,” Newsom said in a statement earlier this month. “But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment.”

Capital punishment is not the simple crime deterrent or solution that the Trump administration has chalked it up to be. Critics of the death penalty argue that, much like the broader criminal justice system, the death penalty disproportionately affects low-income people of color who do not have the best access to good attorneys and potential justice. Generally, people of color are far more likely to be executed by the state than white people, according to a statistic cited by the ACLU.

And all too often, those convictions are not accurate. At least 156 people have been taken off death row since 1973 after it was proven they did not commit the crime. For every 10 death row executions, there’s at least one person exonerated at the national level.

Beyond that, the death penalty is expensive, time-consuming, and all too often completely ineffective. Just this past September, Tennessee inmate Christa Pike survived a second lethal injection attempt, sending her to the hospital on a ventilator and sparking human rights concerns.

items.title: Lawyer Up, JD Vance: Democrats Investigating Vice President
items.content_text:
John Addison—a former gasoline trader at the world’s largest energy and commodity trading company and a massive donor to President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance—secretly met with Vance just days before the Trump administration invaded Venezuela, and even ended up getting a special license to sell Venezuelan crude oil out of it. Now Senate Democrats plan to investigate Vance and Addison.

“I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving ​Venezuelan oil,” wrote Maggie Hassan, New Hampshire Democratic senator (and future Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee chair) in a letter to Vance, according to Reuters.

Earlier this month, the vice president and Addison reportedly met on the tarmac in Bozeman, Montana, and discussed using Addison’s company at the time, Vitol, to sell the oil the Trump administration planned to seize from Venezuela after invading the country and capturing President Nicolás Maduro.

Vance and Addison claim the meeting never happened and that the administration’s selection of Vitol was purely based on merit—and not the fact that Addison donated $300,000 to Vance in 2019 and $7 million to Trump and Trump-supporting groups in 2024.

“Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his ‌private jet ⁠and your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting,” Hassan wrote in her letter. Vance has yet to reply.

This probe is one of many to be expected as Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House, and the Trump administration has given them plenty to investigate. From alleged backroom deals like this in addition to insider trading and pay-to-play schemes, we may be getting a much better look under the hood of the Trump administration next year.

items.title: Trump Sent Vance to Save Jensen Huang’s Butt
items.content_text:
What President Donald Trump wants, he gets. Well, JD Vance gets it for him.

Over the weekend, Trump sent Vance to persuade Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reports. After checking in with Attorney General Todd Blanche, Vance set off to persuade the board, telling them that the U.S. government didn’t view Huang as a national security risk, a U.S. official told the Journal.

Trump isn’t being coy about his role in Huang’s triumphant return. He told CNBC earlier Monday that he “made the deal” to reinstate Huang, and said that he spoke to the board both “directly and indirectly.”

The president also assured Nvidia’s leadership that there was no national security threat. “We gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot,” Trump told CNBC.

Vance was purportedly tapped for the task because of his Silicon Valley connections. The vice president worked in venture capital there after graduating from law school, and is close with Peter Thiel and other tech billionaires.

Being trusted with this negotiation seems to mean a lot to Vance: Trump mentioned Vance’s role briefly in his interview with CNBC, saying that he was “dealing with a vice president, JD Vance, who’s great.” Vance proudly reshared the clip on X.

items.title: Two States Sue Elon Musk’s AI Company Over Deepfake Porn
items.content_text:
Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company is being sued by two states for “nudification”—allowing users to create sexually explicit images of adults and children without their consent.

On Monday, Oregon and Virginia each filed separate complaints against Musk’s SpaceXSI—which operates his Grok artificial intelligence chatbot—for purposefully weakening its regulations against “nudification” and allowing users to create nonconsensual pornographic images of people with relative ease.

In late 2025, X users started posting pictures of different people and asking Grok to take all of their clothes off and/or place them in sexual positions. Grok obliged, creating more than 1.8 million sexually explicit images in barely over a week.

The AI tool even admitted to doing this, writing in January that it “identified lapses in safeguards and [was] urgently fixing them—[child sexual abuse material] is illegal and prohibited … a company could face criminal or civil penalties if it knowingly facilitates or fails to prevent AI-generated CSAM after being alerted.”

That’s exactly what’s happening now, as two states are taking action. Musk and SpaceXSI have previously been sued by 16 other plaintiffs, including the city of Baltimore. President Trump’s Justice Department has already taken Musk’s side on the issue, arguing in August that the blame should solely be on the users, not the creator of the tool.

items.title: Did Trump Profit From Reinstating Jensen Huang?
items.content_text:
From the moment President Trump was first told, in October 2025, that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang stumbled into a Chinese honey trap, Trump didn’t want to hear it. We know that because Trump later claimed not to remember being told, and after receiving that information he did nothing. Trump later claimed also not to remember being told a second time in May 2026 (by Secretary of State Marco Rubio) just before Huang joined Trump on Air Force One to fly to China.* In all likelihood, Trump was told three or more times that Huang was in bed with a Chinese asset named Alice Huang (no relation). Trump didn’t want to hear it because Trump himself was in bed with Jensen.

He still is. Defying, with growing boldness, national security concerns, multiple government investigations, and basic principles of corporate governance, Trump took Huang’s side and pressured Nvidia to reinstate him as chief executive. On November 23, Nvidia gave in to the pressure and, by a unanimous vote, did so.

Never mind that we don’t yet know whether Jensen actively collaborated with Alice to move advanced artificial intelligence chips, illegally, into China, as seems entirely possible. Never mind that we know Jensen had an affair with one of Nvidia’s biggest customers (Alice), and also with one and perhaps two of his employees. These sexual relationships were a clear violation of Nvidia’s conflict of interest policy, which defines “conflict of interest” as “any situation in which an employee or person related to the employee has any actual or apparent personal benefit that may tend to conflict with the fulfillment of the employee’s impartial obligations to NVIDIA.” Such as shagging the staff.

Trump wasn’t the only one demanding Huang’s reinstatement. So, too, did various tech chief executives and former chief executives, including Elon Musk of Tesla and Space X, Sam Altman of Open AI, Gary Tan of Y Combinator, Travis Kalanick of Atoms (formerly Uber), and Steve Chen of YouTube. They co-signed a letter advancing the risible argument that the board itself had “a massive conflict of interest” in removing Huang because doing so “helps their personal legal defense” in a shareholder lawsuit (Vanegas v. Huang) that alleges the board moved far too slowly to remove Huang (which of course it did). Never mind that rehiring Huang will now expose the Nvidia board to many more shareholder lawsuits. “The mistake has been corrected,” Musk announced on X after Huang’s reinstatement.

Nvidia’s statement announcing Huang’s reinstatement made clear that it was doing Trump’s bidding, not Silicon Valley’s. “In the process of reaching its decision,” Nvidia said, “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Trump isn’t hesitating to take credit. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC shortly after Nvidia announced Huang’s return. “And I convinced them. I made the deal.” The board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” Trump said, “and we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.” Keep in mind that when Trump initially claimed not to know the first thing about the espionage allegations he accepted Jensen’s word that he’d never imagined Alice was a spy.

Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan of The New York Times report that Trump decided last week “he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his old job back … despite concerns from his own national security agencies.” Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to contact Huang and the board, which Vance did over the weekend. Vance supplied the board assurances that “the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.”

But what exactly is meant by “the Trump administration”? The Times reports that “only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations,” so it’s doubtful the people in possession of pertinent information were consulted. “The attorney general of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct,” Trump said on Truth Social. That’s no surprise; if the Justice Department possessed such evidence, Huang would already be indicted. What Todd Blanche, the attorney general in question and Trump’s former criminal defense attorney, did not say was that Huang is no longer under investigation. Though given what a Trump lackey Blanche can be, it would not surprise me to learn that Blanche shut down DOJ’s Huang investigation at Trump’s explicit or implied request.

It’s a common misconception among billionaires that the stock market is the same thing as the economy. Trump thinks so, too. As it happens, the Nvidia affair and some disappointment about Anthropic’s IPO tanked the stock market last week. As I write, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq are roaring back, and Nvidia stock is up more than 30 percent. Trump can legitimately take credit. We’ll see how long the boomlet lasts.

One crucial question going forward is whether Trump bought Nvidia stock on the dip before he persuaded Nvidia to rehire Huang. We’ve seen lots of Nvidia stock trades by Trump before. According to CNBC, Trump has bought and sold Nvidia stock at least 103 times since he returned to the White House, with transactions valued between $27 million and $97.5 million.

The White House press office has stated repeatedly that Trump’s stock trades are handled without his input by independent advisers. Trump officials have had to state this repeatedly because nobody believes it. The reasons nobody believes are: (1) the funds are not in a blind trust; (2) it’s hard to imagine Trump ever taking his eyes off his money; and (3), the volume of Trump’s trades far exceeds the norm for an independent money manager. According to Bloomberg, Trump made 28,700 trades between January 21, 2025 and June 30, 2026. That’s more than all stock trades made by House and Senate members, combined, during that same period—and members of Congress are notorious for trading on inside government information.

Trump claims not to remember when Rubio briefed him, back in May 2026, about suspicions that Huang’s girlfriend was spying for China.* Here’s something else Trump will probably claim not to remember: Five days after Rubio grabbed Trump by the collar, Trump sold somewhere between $500,000 and $1 million in Nvidia stock.

I give it at least an even chance that we’ll encounter evidence that Trump pressured Nvidia to rehire Huang not only to boost the broad stock market, but also to boost his personal portfolio. It would fit with the kind of financial self-dealing that already has Democrats feeling impatient to begin investigating. Trump is obliged to file disclosures on his stock trades roughly once a month, so we should know by January 1 whether my cynicism is justified. If Trump did buy a lot of Nvidia stock before Huang’s reinstatement, add that to the articles of impeachment for the House to take up. Third time’s the charm.

* This article originally misidentified the year.

items.title: The $25 Million Reason Why Trump Didn’t Fire Howard Lutnick
items.content_text:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was on the verge of getting pink-slipped—until he gave the president a whole lot of cash.

Lutnick saved his own job with a simple cash infusion of $25 million toward Donald Trump’s presidential library, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday. That detail was first reported by Maggie Haberman in her book Regime Change, which she co-authored with fellow New York Times journalist Jonathan Swan. Haberman added to the Journal’s story on Sunday, sharing on X that Trump had brought up the donation in several big meetings, oftentimes saying that the only reason he tolerated Lutnick’s “bullshit” was because Lutnick “gave me” $25 million.

“Other times he said only that he asked and Lutnick gave it ‘in one second,’” Haberman reported.

Lutnick has been a steadfast component of Trump’s entourage since the 2020 presidential election, when the former Cantor Fitzgerald chairman and lifelong Democrat became one of Trump’s biggest fundraisers. By 2024, Lutnick had become such a trusted confidant in MAGA world that he was appointed as co-chair of Trump’s presidential transition team and, later, tapped to run the Department of Commerce.

But a rift opened between Trump and Lutnick earlier this year, when the latter admitted to lawmakers on Capitol Hill that he visited Jeffrey Epstein’s island in 2012.

Prior to that point, Lutnick had repeatedly rejected Epstein and his crimes, telling the New York Post podcast last year that he cut off all contact with “that disgusting person” after he and his wife were invited to tour Epstein’s Upper East Side townhouse in 2005. Epstein was, at the time, the Lutnicks’ Manhattan neighbor.

But emails made public in an Epstein files document dump indicated that wasn’t true. Instead, Lutnick continued to reach out to the controversial financier, long after Epstein was convicted of sex crimes. One notable occasion included Lutnick’s attendance at one of Epstein’s dinner parties in 2011, which reportedly included other high profile New York socialites, such as alleged child molester (and famed Hollywood filmmaker) Woody Allen, according to government records. Lutnick and Epstein also shared business interests, and even invested in a company together shortly after the island visit.

Trump, who Epstein famously referred to as one of his “closest friends,” must have thought Lutnick’s affiliation was a bad look. But apparently anything can fly in this administration—if the price is right.

items.title: Trump Puts the Brakes on Toxic Lead Detonation in Iowa
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump has called off a detonation of old explosives that would have showered parts of Iowa with toxic lead dust.

Trump posted a rambling message to Truth Social Monday, stating that he had ordered the U.S. Army not to move forward with the plan to destroy deteriorating explosives stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump wrote.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit had temporarily halted the detonation after environmental groups sued, but the Army invoked emergency legal powers to bypass the court order and was still planning to go ahead with the explosion, which was initially scheduled for Monday and then delayed to Wednesday.

The New York Times reported last week that the Army had rejected an alternative for destroying the explosives that would not have carried the same risk of lead dust. Any tactic for getting rid of the deteriorating explosives comes with risks; the Army said that the cleaner option would require military personnel to handle the explosives, making them more likely to explode at random and put its handlers in danger.

Why did the Army not clean up these barrels of lead azide before they became so dangerous? The Times said it was “unclear.” Trump blamed Obama.

“In 2009, the Obama Administration improperly stored a vast number of explosives, and the Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future. We have an opportunity to do a highly controlled detonation of these dangerous and rapidly corroding materials,” he wrote.

He also was sure to clarify that if the old explosives did accidentally detonate, it wasn’t his fault—it’s the court’s fault, or the fault of Democratic Governor-Elect Rob Sand.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump concluded.

items.title: What “Tough Incident” Did Trump Help Elon Musk With?
items.content_text:
While doing a victory lap to celebrate the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, President Trump also admitted to helping out another one of his billionaire friends: Elon Musk.

“You know I protected Elon in my first term, very big. Elon was protected,” Trump said Monday on CNBC, comparing it to his protection of Huang. “I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon, I love Elon, he’s great. 80 percent supergenius, 20 percent he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon I protected, you wouldn’t have an Elon if it wasn’t for me … a certain incident took place, a tough incident … we have to protect our brilliant people, because we don’t have enough … they’re national treasures.”

Trump did not elaborate as to what exactly that “tough incident” he protected Musk from during his first term was, even as the billionaire was particularly active during that period—founding Neuralink and the Boring Company, as well as endorsing Andrew Yang and later voting for Joe Biden for president. Regardless, bragging about helping two of the most powerful CEOs in the world avoid accountability for their actions is not something the president of the United States should be doing—at least not publicly.

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s Ex-Chief of Staff Says He Should Resign
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s former top aide is calling for him to step down.

“Pete’s been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service,” Joe Kasper told Politico Monday.

Kasper, who was Hegseth’s chief of staff for the first three months of the second Trump administration, cited a number of reasons: Hegseth’s mishandling of the war in Iran, his mismanagement of the Pentagon, and how his own bluster and pride have prevented him from doing his job.

The secretary of defense “overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement,” Kasper said.

In response, a senior Pentagon official told Politico that they weren’t surprised that a “disgruntled former staffer … is now peddling made-up gossip to the media.

“Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr. Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure,” the official said.

In his telling, Kasper was moved to call for Hegseth’s resignation after the secretary’s group was scolded for laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day. He said that he realized within a week of starting at the Pentagon in 2025 that his boss’s focus was all about himself, “rather than the institution and the men and women who support it.”

“There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship,” Kasper told Politico. “The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them [even] less so now.”

Kasper added that between firings and resignations, the Pentagon’s top brass had been all but hollowed out. Kasper said that the Army was “essentially leaderless,” and that “at almost every high-profile position, or every senior leader position, there’s a vacancy.”

Hegseth has so far managed to cling on to his position, surviving an impeachment vote earlier this month, but he could be in for a rude awakening come January.

“I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be,” Kasper said.

items.title: “Sex Sells”: Trump Says Jensen Huang’s Affairs Are Actually Good
items.content_text:
Donald Trump seems to believe that Jensen Huang’s scandalous affair will actually improve his career.

Huang resumed his roles as Nvidia’s president, chief executive officer, and member of the board Monday morning. The board of directors said that their decision to ignore the billionaire’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the subsequent national security concerns were based on influential conversations with “senior levels of the United States government.”

Trump phoned in to CNBC to take credit for his part in the psyop moments after the company announced Huang’s reappointment, noting that he personally assured the board both “directly and indirectly” that Huang was not a national security risk. But in the midst of bragging about throwing around the weight of the U.S. government, Trump also let slip that he believed the Nvidia exec’s foreign entanglement would benefit Huang in the long run.

“I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level,” Trump told the business network. “He apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate.”

“That was probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas,” Trump said. “Sex sells.”

“He’s apologized for that, to the company, to the country, to his family and his wife,” Trump continued, taking a beat to compliment Huang’s wife. “And they’ve accepted and I think everyone’s accepted.”

“I actually think it could be—I mean it sounds strange—but I think it could be a net positive. People are realizing how the job he’s done, and put—it was a terrible spotlight in one way, but in another way it showed how advanced this company is, how incredibly advanced it is with respect to chips.”

“I think he’s gonna be at a similar level to what he was. I don’t think he’s going to be diminished at all. I think people respect what he’s gone through, and he’s handled it very well,” Trump said.

Shortly after the interview concluded, Trump shared an artificial intelligence–generated image on his Truth Social account of Huang’s face photoshopped onto the famous photograph of Trump raising his fist after he was shot in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024. Only, Huang’s variant had the CEO holding a red bra over his head, with an Nvidia branded flag behind him.

Huang was effectively forced out of Nvidia earlier this month after reports emerged that he had had several affairs, including two with Nvidia employees and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset.

Trump reportedly knew about the affair for months, but did nothing to mitigate the potential national security risks. Instead, Trump only got involved when the situation started to turn south for Huang, and Nvidia’s stock prices as a result.

Nvidia shares spiraled in the weeks after Huang was ousted from the company he co-founded, rattling the U.S. economy and Trump’s personal stock portfolio with it. The president’s 2026 financial disclosures revealed that he purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock earlier this year.

But few in Washington appear to be on the same page as Trump about Huang’s grand return to Silicon Valley. Several lawmakers from both sides of the aisle criticized the board’s decision shortly after it was announced, arguing that congressional investigations into Huang’s attachments and Nvidia’s potentially compromised environment must proceed.

This story has been updated.

items.title: GOP Rep.: Congress Can Trade Stocks Because D.C. is “Not Corrupt”
items.content_text:
One Republican representative has a very basic argument against banning stock trading: It’s just, like, not even necessary!

“They’re trying to make it seem like Washington is corrupt,” Representative Pete Sessions said on Newsmax Monday morning. “Washington is not corrupt.”

Phew, I was getting worried there for a second!

Soon-to-be Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday that passing a bill banning stock trading among lawmakers would be one of the Democrats’ first priorities in the new year, stressing that Democrats had to “clean up the mess in Washington,” starting with Congress.

“Which is why very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock,” Jeffries said on CBS’s Face the Nation.

In September, the House passed a bill that would prevent lawmakers from buying new individual stocks, but wouldn’t require them to sell the stocks they already own. The bill didn’t pass the Senate, with Democrats arguing that it didn’t go far enough to actually solve the problem.

However, even if Democrats were to pass a stronger version of the bill, it wouldn’t touch the corrupter-in-chief: President Donald Trump, who has become much, much richer through stock trading, including shares of Nvidia, for which he loosened export restrictions and then reaped the benefits.

Regardless, come January, Sessions’s assertion that “Washington isn’t corrupt” may quickly be put to the test, as Senator Elizabeth Warren and fellow Democrats have indicated that they will be launching investigations into Trump, his family members, and members of the administration for their potentially corrupt business dealings. We’ll all have to wait and see what they find.

items.title: Could Democrats Trick Trump Into Improving Health Care?
items.content_text:
There’s a “real possibility” that President Trump compromises with the Democratic congressional majority on health care, he said during a press conference on Friday.

“There’s a real possibility that we get a lotta great things done, especially on health care,” Trump told reporters. “I’m open to great health care. Now, can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want—and we could end up with great health care in our country. We can end up better than dealing with the Republicans.”

This sudden openness to bipartisanship came after Michigan Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed framed his support for Medicare for All as “Trumpcare,” complete with a mocked-up image of a golden health insurance card, in a post earlier this month—which Trump then reposted on his Truth Social account Saturday. El-Sayed responded by doubling down on his campaign for universal health care over the weekend.

“Well, the president signaled openness to the opportunity, and you know I played lacrosse growing up, and I was always taught that you play the ball, not the man,” he said on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday. “My job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country health care.”

“Trumpcare for All would save the average American thousands of dollars a month. You just care more about protecting Big Insurance and Big Pharma to admit it,” El-Sayed posted on X Sunday, responding to Republican Senator Rand Paul’s criticism of universal health care. “Donald, come get your boy.”

Trump seems to be responding positively to El-Sayed’s proposition, likely because it has the president’s name on it. And as the Michigan Senator-elect has said, it doesn’t really matter what they call it—as long as Americans don’t have to choose between good health and financial ruin anymore.

items.title: Republicans Bash Nvidia’s Insane Decision to Bring Back Jensen Huang
items.content_text:
American lawmakers are less than thrilled about Jensen Huang’s sudden reappointment atop Nvidia.

Huang resumed his roles as president, chief executive officer, and member of the board Monday morning following a decision by the company’s board of directors, which cited influential conversations with “senior levels of the United States government” as part of its rationale to effectively ignore the billionaire’s scandalous affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

In a statement, the board claimed that it was “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Many of the country’s elected officials, however, did not share the same feeling.

“You gotta be kidding me!” remarked Texas Senator John Cornyn as he received news of Huang’s reappointment from MS NOW’s Mychael Schnell.

Cornyn followed up separately on X, writing, “No national security risk? Based on what?”

Florida Senator Rick Scott said the fiasco looked “terrible on its face.”

Nebraska Representative Don Bacon also came down hard on the multitrillion-dollar semiconductor company, arguing that Huang was “compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy.”

“Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang,” Bacon posted on X. “Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible.”

Prior to his unexpected return, Huang had agreed to meet with several congressional bodies to explain the details of his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset. Huang is still scheduled to appear for closed-door interviews on December 1, and to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee at a yet-to-be determined date.

Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren described Huang’s rehire as “reckless” in a conversation with Reuters, adding that the decision does not change the reality that Huang and Nvidia’s board and executives are expected to provide answers to Congress regarding its compliance with U.S. exports.

“The Trump Administration also ​needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given ​and by ⁠which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement,” Warren said. “Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan ⁠export ​control bills into law and making sure ​NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security ​at risk.”

Nebraska Senator Pete Ricketts similarly condemned Huang’s reappointment, sharing his anecdotal experience on X: “I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips,” Ricketts continued. “I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Michigan Representative Debbie Dingell slammed the company’s decision to move forward without that critical information—and before finishing its own internal investigation.

“Nvidia’s board made an irresponsible decision to reinstate Jensen Huang before Congress has even heard from him,” she noted on X. “There are serious national security questions that still need to be answered. The board must explain why it was willing to move ahead without those answers.”

Republican Senator Kevin Cramer remarked that the board’s decision had placed not only the company in an extremely tenuous position, but the entirety of the United States, as well.

“The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Cramer wrote on social media, urging Congress to pass the strictest export controls possible in light of Huang’s rehire. “The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know.”

But the president could not hide his enthusiasm. In a post on Truth Social Monday morning, Donald Trump claimed that Nvidia’s board had “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump said. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

Nvidia’s stock spiraled in the weeks after Huang was ousted from the company he co-founded, rattling the U.S. economy with it. But Trump’s interest in Nvidia stems beyond the broad scope of the economy: The president’s 2026 financial disclosures revealed that he purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock earlier this year.

“The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom,” posted Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego.

The White House was apparently proud to share news of Trump’s intimate involvement in the process, which basically amounted to the president personally overstepping an existing national security threat and an independent company’s internal HR concerns to restabilize the stock market and benefit of his own pocketbook.

“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami.

A total of at least eight GOP senators have spoken up on the matter by the time of publication.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Trump’s Smithsonian Takeover Plan Accidentally Revealed on Train
items.content_text:
A Trump administration staffer may have accidentally exposed the grand takeover of the Smithsonian museum network while riding on the Washington, D.C. metro system.

Last month, a passenger on the metro’s orange line saw a man in a suit using a laptop that had a 25-point “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan” displayed prominently on his screen. It included plans to fire director Anthea Hartig and her staff as well as build a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington, putting up an “exciting cool exhibit on D-Day,” and creating a new politically charged permanent exhibit titled “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance.”

The plans also included a total reconfiguration of the museum’s K-12 programming to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The rider sent pictures of the staffer’s screen to ProPublica, and the staffer in question was revealed to be Sam Bock, 27, an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council.

While the White House has yet to respond, these alleged plans align with essentially every other policy position they’ve taken against the museum network. Trump has been at war with the Smithsonian for the entirety of his second tenure, using his “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History” executive order to delegitimize anything remotely honest or critical about the history of this country, claiming that the Smithsonian had been captured “by a radical, activist ideology that is fundamentally opposed to telling the noble, honest story of the great country we know and love.”

This, along with Trump’s efforts to take over the Kennedy Center, have made it clear that this agenda for American landmarks and museums are more about controlling the narrative than it is about an honest retelling of American history.

items.title: Trump Successfully Begs for Jensen Huang’s Return
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump’s plea to have his friend Jensen Huang back in the driver’s seat at Nvidia has been answered.

On Sunday, the president posted on Truth Social, “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Hours later on Monday morning, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang was being reinstated as CEO.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, the board’s chair, in a press release. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.

The president has hinted multiple times that he wants to see Huang reinstated. Trump urged Huang to resist pressure to leave the company, and repeatedly told reporters that he’d prefer if Huang was brought back in, from saying he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang remained as CEO to asking the board for a “second chance.”

Trump’s post Sunday night also came right after a new New York Times report revealed that Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with, was in contact with China’s top spy agency while they were seeing each other. Nvidia is continuing to investigate Huang’s relationship, per the press release.

The president’s stake in Nvidia has ballooned in the past couple of years, at the same time as his policy decisions—like allowing Nvidia to sell to China—boosted the company’s profits. It’s hard to take Trump at his word that this would be the “best thing … for the U.S.A.” and not just the best thing for him—but Nvidia’s board evidently agrees.

items.title: Nvidia Board Brings Back Jensen Huang in Dumbest Move Ever
items.content_text:
Money talks, even if it’s complicated by a Chinese spy campaign.

In a stunning twist, Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated Jensen Huang as its president, chief executive officer, and member of the board Monday. The decision was effective immediately.

An announcement from the company’s board claimed that Huang’s involvement with the company was not a national security risk, citing conversations with “senior levels of the United States government.” It did not make clear who those government individuals were.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said board chair Harvey C. Jones in a statement. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.”

Huang was effectively forced out of the company he co-founded earlier this month after reports emerged that he had had several affairs, including two with Nvidia employees and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no relation of Jensen’s), a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a spy and a state asset.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement following the board’s announcement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

“I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support,” he continued. “Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Nvidia has emerged in recent years as the largest semiconductor company in the world, and a precious American asset in the burgeoning AI tech wave. But in the midst of Huang’s scandal, it appeared there was only one key player in the U.S. government fighting for him to remain atop the multi-trillion dollar company: Donald Trump.

Trump reportedly knew about Huang’s affair—and the allegations against his partner—for months. State Secretary Marco Rubio informed Trump about the alarming relationship moments before Huang joined the presidential trip to Beijing at the president’s request. It was at least the second time that Trump had been informed of Huang’s ties to the Chinese government, reported The New York Times.

But Trump did not act on the information.

Instead, Trump has repeatedly denied any knowledge of the illicit affair. At a White House press conference earlier this month, Trump refuted the Times’s report, telling a reporter that he “didn’t hear about” the scandal in May. Trump added that he spoke with Huang earlier that day, remarking that he “really believed” Huang’s claim that he had “absolutely no idea” that his former Chinese affair partner was a spy.

In a post on Truth Social Monday morning, Trump claimed that Nvidia’s board had “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump said. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

The White House was apparently proud to share news of Trump’s involvement in the process, which included personally dialing in to Nvidia’s board meeting to argue for Huang’s return.

“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami.

Other parts of the Trump administration have failed to defend Huang with the same fervor (or total delusion) as the president. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton—who is supposed to be one of the most informed individuals on critical government intelligence in the country—only learned about Alice Huang’s location from ABC News anchor Jonathan Karl on Sunday. In a brief exchange in which he appeared remarkably disinterested in the maneuverings of the spy who was seriously intimate with the head of one of America’s biggest tech companies, Clayton simply responded “oh” after hearing the breaking development.

In another TV appearance on Fox News Sunday, Clayton admitted that “there are chips that have ended up in places they should not.”

But Republican Senator John Kennedy summed up the whole ordeal best. In an interview with NBC News’s Meet the Press, Kennedy described Huang’s scandal as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.”

This story has been updated.

items.title: Transcript: Trump Lets Slip How Putin Manipulates Him in Epic Self-Own
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 23 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump’s summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping is getting widely pilloried in the press for accomplishing just about nothing. And speaking to reporters, Trump accidentally revealed exactly how Putin and Xi manipulated him at the gathering, by skillfully playing on his ego in all kinds of embarrassing ways. All this tells us a lot about what to expect from the next two years.

So we’re unraveling what really happened over there with foreign policy expert Elizabeth Saunders, who’s been arguing for Foreign Affairs that a lame-duck Trump can still do tremendous damage internationally. Elizabeth, thanks for coming on.

Elizabeth Saunders: Thanks for having me.

Sargent: So let’s start here. The press coverage of this has been absolutely savage. The Associated Press called it a fleeting photo op. Trump legitimized Putin’s claim that he wants peace in Ukraine, which is preposterous, and handed China a major victory, even as we’re discovering that China may have spied on American AI. Elizabeth, what exactly did Trump accomplish at this summit?

Saunders: I think you summed it up well in one word: nothing, except damaging photo ops. And so there were things he might have tried to do, like put pressure on Putin to end the war in Ukraine, to continue talking to China about rare earths. In the end, he just did photo ops, because he doesn’t put in the diplomatic legwork. Number one.

And number two, he’s not interested in putting pressure on Russia, because he’s friends with Putin, and that’s all he really cares about. And same with Xi. So for him, he’s cozying up to authoritarians, and that means not doing anything that will put them ill at ease and actually advance an agenda.

Sargent: Right. Not only did he not pressure Putin to end the war in Ukraine, he actually relaxed the pressure on Putin to end the war in Ukraine. Isn’t that what happened?

Saunders: Absolutely. And on the way home, he called the European leaders. He dialed in to their meeting and said Putin wants to end the war, and you should really stop aiding Ukraine. And that is just contrary to what’s in the American national interest.

It’s contrary to any sort of understanding about American values and interests abroad. It’s clearly contradictory to what the Europeans want and the Ukrainians want, but Trump just doesn’t care. He likes Putin and considers him a friend, and he doesn’t see that his interests and the American interests ought to be aligned.

Sargent: Just to clarify for people, what you’re talking about here is that there were reports after the summit that Trump called in from Air Force One, called European leaders, and essentially told them that they could save money and save lives by ending the war with Russia. He more or less pressured them to stop aiding Ukraine.

That’s what essentially seems to have happened, which is just so contrary to what’s in the interests of the Western alliance, it almost can’t even be quantified, can it?

Saunders: Absolutely. But the problem is, Trump doesn’t believe in the Western alliance, right? His three lodestars when it comes to foreign policy: He doesn’t like multilateral trade deals. He doesn’t like alliances. And he loves authoritarian rulers.

And so the summit sort of captures all of it, right? He didn’t bother to put in the legwork to complete the Thailand trade deal, which was even just bilateral. He had the hugs with Xi and the handshake with Putin, cozying up to authoritarians. And he did things that were completely not in the interest of America’s longtime allies. It’s really quite shocking.

Sargent: It really is. And speaking to reporters, Trump let out an aside about Putin that was pretty revealing. Here he’s talking about Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. He says he privately asked Putin a question about this. Listen.

Donald Trump (voiceover): I actually asked him. I said, would you have gone in if I was president? He said, no. Would never happen. It was handled so badly. By our country, it’s handled very badly.


Sargent: So what Trump means by this is, Joe Biden handled things so badly that Putin felt free to invade Ukraine. And Trump claims Putin privately assured him that he couldn’t have done that if Trump were president.

Elizabeth, presuming for now that this is true, which it could be, given how Putin has Trump’s number, this is exactly how Putin manipulates Trump, by flattering his belief that he’s strong, just like Putin is, right?

Saunders: Absolutely. And what does Putin have to lose by saying something like that? He’s already invaded, so—he’s heard Trump say this 50 times on television: It never would have happened if I’d been president. So maybe he didn’t say it, but it’s totally plausible that he would try to manipulate Trump by saying, I would never have invaded if it’d been you in charge.

Sargent: Well, let’s listen to another one of Trump’s exchanges with a reporter. It really underscores what’s going on here. It’s about Trump’s frequent description of Putin as a friend, which he reiterated at the summit. Check this out.

Reporter (voiceover): While you were there, you said that Putin is your friend. Russia, of course, is Iran’s biggest ally. Do you believe Putin is a friend to America?

Trump (voiceover): I can’t speak to America. I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. And to be honest, he was very nice about it. It was a rigged hoax. It was a hoax that was made up by the Democrats. It probably helped me win the election, rewin the election. And I consider him to be somebody that have a very good relationship.


Sargent: Note there how Trump has nothing to say about whether Putin and Russia’s various stances benefit the American national interest. He only says that Putin was good to him.

Here again, it’s laid entirely bare how Putin manipulates Trump, and Trump basically admits straight out that how Putin treats him personally is more important to him than how our country fares out of all of this. Your thoughts on that?

Saunders: Well, to me, what’s so revealing about that clip is that Trump actually says out loud that he can’t speak to whether Putin is a friend to America, right? He has always cared about how Putin treats him personally, but his job is to represent the American people and American national interests.

That’s what we hired him to do—we, as in the voters. That was the verdict in 2024. And his job is to go and represent American interests. And he’s literally saying in this clip that whether Putin is a friend to America doesn’t matter to him.

Sargent: It’s an extraordinary faceplant moment, especially when you take it with the other one. It just could not be clearer how he has zero conception of how this relationship with Putin actually affects our country.

What’s the right answer to the question Trump was asked? What should he say when asked whether Russia is a friend to the United States? What’s the best way to explain the right answer to the American people?

Saunders: Well, the right answer is “no.” Putin is not a friend to the American people. He’s not a friend to Europe. He is promoting violence—I mean, he’s committing violence in Ukraine, and he’s promoting violence, if not behind it, in European countries.

He is a threat to Europe, and he’s a threat to American interests. I worry that we’ve all become so numb to this, but the answer is “No, Putin is not a friend to the United States.”

Sargent: Well, let’s listen to one more short snippet from Trump, this time talking about China.

Trump (voiceover): President Xi met our country—didn’t meet me, met our country—at the plane, something he’s never done before. And that means he respects our country. He didn’t meet Sleepy Joe at the plane, that I can tell you.

Sargent: So Xi meets our country at the plane. He’d never do that for Sleepy Joe. This shows he respects Trump’s America. What do you make of Trump’s conception of international respect there?

Saunders: I think it shows tremendous canniness on Xi’s part, because he knows all Trump cares about is the red carpet and the trappings, right? And so I don’t think that Xi—I don’t think he ever did meet Biden’s plane, but that’s because he respected the U.S. presidency. He wouldn’t bother to try that on a Joe Biden, right? Or a Barack Obama. It’s quite striking how Xi and Putin both have Trump’s number.

And it’s also striking that in the same news conference, Trump complained about Canada and said that they’ve been very unfair to us for 50 years, and we’re not going to tolerate that anymore. What we have is a through-the-looking-glass foreign policy. We are still, all these years later, watching the president of the United States attack our allies, undermine our allies and friends, and cozy up to dictators.

Sargent: Richard Stengel, a former State Department official, made a very similar point to what you’re saying there. He tweeted the following: “China sees Trump as a chump. Can you imagine any other American president having a summit with China the week after it was revealed that Chinese espionage was threatening our national security?”

Saunders: I think it’s worse than that. I think the Nvidia scandal is far more serious in terms of national security than I think we’ve even grasped. I think the other problem with the summit is, yes, it was basically a nothingburger in terms of substance. And yes, these photo ops legitimize authoritarian regimes, and that’s very dangerous. But I think the other thing it does is, it just allows these dictators to continue to run the clock, right?

And especially in the case of Russia and Putin in Ukraine, it’s allowing Putin to spin this along for another winter and take another year to potentially continue the war. And Trump doesn’t understand that this talking during war can be quite dangerous and give Russia a chance to catch up and regroup.

And with China, you know, he’s just allowing Xi to make preparations, military preparations, and do things with the economy that the United States might not really want.

And so I do think the opportunity cost is something we don’t really think about. You know, these summits don’t come around very often. And if you don’t think you’re going to get anything done, maybe just don’t go, right? And other presidents have just decided not to go. So I really worry that there’s actually a real hidden cost to what we just witnessed.

Sargent: Well, yes, Trump doesn’t have any conception of getting something done for the country. He just sees this as getting something done for himself, which maybe it did in some ways, at least to certain parts of the country, I don’t know. But it’s correct, as Richard Stengel says, that China sees Trump as a chump, right?

Saunders: Absolutely right.

Sargent: In exactly this way. Like, China gets that the pomp and the pageantry is all Trump cares about. They know he just suffered the most dramatic repudiation in a midterm election in half a century. They know that he’s desperate to feel a little stronger and look a little stronger, and they just milked the shit out of it, basically, didn’t they?

Saunders: Worse than that. I mean, I think it’s not just that it accomplished nothing, it’s that it accomplished a lot for Xi and Putin, right? They gained a lot just by standing still. And I think that’s part of what their goal was, right? And they knew it would be easy. It was easy.

They didn’t have to do a whole lot, right? There was almost no contention that has been reported. And so just by delivering the pomp, they buy themselves a lot of time to do things that are against American interests.

And I think the fact that Trump sort of blessed this, by sitting in for those pictures and coming back and giving a news conference where he’s talking about how great the whole thing was, and how great it was that Xi Jinping met him at the plane—it’s harming, actively harming, American interests. It’s not just a failed or nothingburger summit.

Sargent: Right. Well, just to go big picture: Russia and China do see themselves as usurping American power in the world, as Ed Wong wrote recently. China especially believes Trump is presiding over a declining American empire.
