Putin very likely believes he’s made real strides in weakening the United States, in the sense that he’s had success in dividing the U.S. from its Western allies, and he surely sees Trump as his useful idiot in doing that. Is this basically the shape of things, more or less what I just said there?

Saunders: Yes, I think that’s exactly right. And I think one thing that Democrats are going to have to realize—or supporters of the Democratic Party, or supporters in the Republican Party of what used to be the sort of garden-variety GOP foreign policy—is that Trump still has two full years, and this is the sphere where he’s going to be able to do the most, or, worse, not do the things that they might want him to do to rebuild alliances and counter Ukraine and so forth.

And so, again, their goal at this summit wasn’t necessarily to get Trump to sign a piece of paper. It was to just tread water so that they can grow and face less resistance from America than they would under virtually any other president that I can think of.

Sargent: Well, speaking of those last two years, what should Democrats in Congress do, recognizing that their powers are somewhat limited in this domain? They do have the power of the purse. They have investigatory power. They really do have a lot of levers here. What can they do to mitigate this damage that he’s doing on these two fronts?

Saunders: Well, I think people have been talking about kind of three different levers. One is the power of the purse. I think that’s the weakest. I think it is very, very hard to actually wield the power of the purse in wartime. A lot of effort went into that in Vietnam, and it repeatedly failed. It’s just not politically popular, even in an unpopular war, to take money away from troops. So I have my doubts about that.

The second would be passing Ukraine legislation. I think that’s maybe the one area where they do maybe have a veto-proof majority. Of course, it’s still the executive branch that has to distribute that money, and that’s what Trump got impeached for the first time: for getting in the way of congressionally appropriated aid to Ukraine, with his perfect phone call.

Sargent: What would legislation look like if Democrats pass something?

Saunders: A big aid package for Ukraine that we haven’t done in a long time, right? And the Republicans might join that. And maybe they wouldn’t, you know. If Trump vetoed it, at that point that would be sort of a come-to-Jesus moment for them, right? Are they really, in this climate, going to vote against aid to Ukraine with Trump kind of on his way out?

Where I do think that the Democrats can have a very, very big effect is in investigating corruption, and in investigating this Nvidia scandal, which is both corruption and national security, right?

If Trump was really told on the flight to Beijing, before they stopped in Alaska—and maybe even before that, depending on the reporting that you look at—that Jensen Huang was having an affair with someone who had links to Chinese intelligence, and then did nothing about it—I can’t think of much anything really in the national security space more serious than that. I mean, the insurrection of January 6 was in some ways more serious, but a very different domain.

That is really an impeachable offense, straight up. And that’s just based off what we know already. And so if they can uncover that, I think it would kill two birds with one stone, in the sense that it would highlight the corruption—because Trump has made so much money, and Howard Lutnick, and the U.S. stake in Nvidia—and also the devastating effects of this second Trump administration on national security and intelligence gathering and just keeping the nation’s secrets and keeping policy on track.

Sargent: That’s actually very heartening stuff. And I think it’s worth remembering that Democrats were really able to make extraordinary headway in putting together what happened with the Trump-Ukraine scandal. And so you can actually see them being able to uncover something extremely, extremely damning, something much more damning than we know with the Nvidia stuff, right?

Saunders: I think so. I think there’s got to be a tremendous amount that we don’t know. I don’t think it will only be Trump who’s implicated. I don’t think it will only be Howard Lutnick that’s implicated. But I think Congress’s investigatory powers could be well spent in that area.

It’s clearly of vital importance to not only geopolitics, but, you know, all of our retirement funds. This is an issue that will resonate politically: the corruption, the effect on the U.S. economy.

And the climate is just very different. The political climate is very different than it was with the first Ukraine impeachment, right? He’s had his last election, and clearly Republicans are starting to pull away from him, and he doesn’t inspire the same level of fear.

I still don’t know that you get 67 votes to convict under pretty much any circumstance, but I do think that, for the sake of what comes after—there’s so much rebuilding that’s going to have to be done on corruption and national security to put us back on sound footing. That would be investigatory effort well spent.

Sargent: Yes. And Trump is a substantially diminished figure relative to the time during the Ukraine scandal. Elizabeth Saunders, it’s going to get really interesting. The Democratic Congress is going to be, I think, a little bit more formidable than people are ready for. It’s big majorities. Elizabeth, thank you so much for coming on.

Saunders: Thanks for having me.

items.title:
Why I’m Nervous as Hell That the
Democrats Are Going to Screw This Up
items.content_text:
1. Sleepwalking

Suddenly, I am gripped with fear that the Democrats are sleepwalking. They have just been handed a mandate from the voters that has few parallels in the last 60 years. That’s great. But with mandates come expectations—expectations of all those people who voted Democratic who usually don’t, and of course of all the people who always and reliably do—that the party will accomplish dramatic things. And the Democrats—especially the Democrats in the United States Senate—don’t appear to have the slightest understanding that they are likely to fail all these voters and clear the path for President Rubio in 2028.

Because the situation is this. In the next Congress, the Democrats will control 56 Senate seats. It’s an amazing number. Amazing. And yet, it is at the same time a meaningless number. Because the only number in the Senate that means anything is 60. That is the number of votes required under Senate rules to end debate on any given measure and move to final passage of a bill. Final passage can be won with 51 votes; but you can’t get to that final passage vote, in most cases, until you win a “cloture” vote of 60 senators.

That means that to do a lot of the things Democrats promised the voters they would do, they’ll need 60 votes under current Senate rules. Which means in turn they’ll need to get four Republicans, and potentially five given John Fetterman’s surly volatility, to side with them on any given matter: undoing the Medicaid cuts, restoring the Obamacare subsidies, raising the minimum wage, doing dozens of other things.

I am worried because I’ve been hearing a lot of happy talk these last couple of weeks. On MS NOW, I hear some Democratic politicians and guests and the occasional host assert the confident view that surely now a chastened Republican minority, so thoroughly thrashed at the polls in November, will be willing to play ball and vote with Democrats. Further down in this piece, we’ll dig into the deep unlikelihood of that in more granular detail.

But for now, I’ll race you to my conclusion, which is grim but based on the irrefutable evidence of recent Senate history: The people making these happy assertions are in fantasy land. Democrats will not get those four votes on almost anything.

Republicans aren’t stupid about this. They’ll talk a great game. They’ll say they want to work with their Democratic friends. And on any given matter, three Republicans willing to end cloture may well emerge.

But that fourth, to get to 60? Please. Imagine yourself a Republican senator. Are you going to give the Democrats their sixtieth vote to restore Obamacare subsidies? Absolutely not. If you do, you are guaranteeing yourself a well-financed primary the next time you run. And don’t think that Fox News can’t count. Well—they can’t count votes out of Arizona, maybe. But they can count to 60, rest assured of that.

So if Ted Budd and Ashley Moody and Lisa Murkowski have said they’d vote to clear cloture on a “Democrat” priority, the right-wing press might give the three of them a pass, because Budd and Moody are up for reelection in 2028, and Murkowski, because she’s Murkowski. But that fourth Republican? He or she will be scalped. In every state, there’s a state legislator or a tech dude or a lumber magnate who lusts to be senator and who is even, impossible as this may seem, more right-wing than the incumbent. Democrats and liberals might think right now that normal, historic, mainstream pressure on GOP senators to play ball will be strong. But the far stronger pressure these next two years, in every state, will come from the right.

The end result? It is this. The House, with an extremely comfortable Democratic margin, will pass all kinds of good things. Then those things will go to the Senate. And you know what will happen? They’ll die. And two years from now, all those people who voted Democratic will be wondering: Why didn’t they do anything? I thought they were gonna do all these big things. Those voters will be angry. They’ll be right to be angry. And the reason will be that the Democrats didn’t do anything about the filibuster.

2. Some Quick History

The history of the filibuster is long and complicated, and there are excellent books you can read about it if you so wish. I won’t go into that history in detail here. But I will evoke portions of that history to bat down specious arguments made today by the filibuster’s defenders.

The first is that the founders intended the Senate to be this way. If you ever hear anyone say that on cable TV, please know instantly that that person is an idiot or a liar. There is no third option. They will invoke George Washington’s line about the Senate being intended as a saucer to “cool the hot tea,” and Washington did indeed say that, and the founders did indeed intend for the Senate to be a slower-moving and more deliberate body than the House of Representatives. And they had solutions for that: It’s why Senate terms are six years and House terms are two, and it’s why senators initially weren’t directly elected by the people.

But the supermajority principle on which the filibuster is based? Most of the founders hated it. After all, they tried it and ditched it—the Articles of Confederation required that nine colonies support any measure, and it was unworkable. As for the Constitution itself, there are several supermajority provisions, but they are specific and they’re all major things: impeachment, overriding a veto, approval of treaties, expulsion of a member. If they thought it should take 60 votes to get a normal piece of legislation through the Senate, wouldn’t they have said so? But they did not.

And they did not because they opposed it. Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton didn’t agree on much. But they agreed on this. Hamilton wrote in the twenty-second Federalist Paper: “To give a minority a negative upon the majority (which is always the case where more than a majority is requisite to a decision) is … to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser number.” He called this “a poison.” A poison.

And Jefferson wrote a manual of parliamentary procedure for the very Senate I’m writing about here. In his manual, written while he was vice president (and therefore president of the Senate), he wrote: “The voice of the majority decides; for the lex majoris partis is the law of all councils, elections, &c., where not otherwise expressly provided.” Lex majoris partis means “the law of the greater part,” and the exceptions Jefferson referred to were the ones specifically spelled out in the Constitution.

And finally, here’s a compelling quote from James Madison, in Federalist 58, explaining why supermajority requirements are anti-democratic:

In all cases where justice or the general good might require new laws to be passed, or active measures to be pursued, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. It would be no longer the majority that would rule; the power would be transferred to the minority.

The founders would have hated the filibuster. Who would have liked it? Slavers, racists, and segregationists. John C. Calhoun was the senator who really started using the filibuster, and he did so to protect slavery. He hated majority rule, because he knew the slaveholding planter class was a minority whose days were numbered. In A Disquisition on Government, published shortly after his 1850 death, he came up with the idea of a “concurrent majority”; it’s a fancy name, and of course it’s dressed in highfalutin finery, but its basic intent was to protect the slavers. The disquisition was a direct assault on Madison.

The filibuster went through a number of changes, and there were several key dates or eras—the 1850s, the 1890s, the first World War, when the current “Rule 22” was written, and the civil-rights era, when Southern racists filibustered civil rights and anti-lynching laws. But for present-day relevance, the key change came in 1975.

That was the year the Senate lowered the cloture threshold from 67 votes to 60. It seemed like a good reform at the time. But it ended up having a pernicious effect. When the threshold was 67, everyone knew that the filibuster was to be threatened only in very unusual circumstances. But when it was lowered to 60, senators became more casual about it. A threat of a filibuster by the minority became more common, which led to the majorities having to invoke the cloture process (which by the way is complicated and has various stages and is not simply about the one vote to end debate).

This just predated the age of polarization, which had its roots in the 1980s. Combining the two—the 1975 rule change and galloping polarization—meant that filibuster threats became routine, which forced cloture to be invoked far more frequently than it had been. Look at this eye-popping chart. In 1973–74, 44 cloture motions were filed. In 1993–94, the number was 80. In 2013–14, it was 252. And in 2023–24, it was 266.

This is paralysis. And it is a jillion miles away from what the founders intended. Any serious person knows this deep down.

3. The Bogus Arguments Against Eliminating the Filibuster

Democrats who are afraid to kill or reform the filibuster make a few basic arguments. Their first argument, I’ve already dealt with: that the founders would have approved. They clearly would not have.

A second argument is that eliminating the filibuster would increase partisanship. This is as accepted a piece of conventional wisdom as exists in Washington, but it’s utterly wrong; exactly backwards. A Senate with no filibuster would on balance be a far more bipartisan place. If the minority knows that the majority can pass something with 51 votes, then a few of them will be far more likely to play ball and seek compromise. Well hell, if the damn thing’s gonna pass anyway, maybe I should get an amendment in there or get a project for my state.

Not every minority senator would think like this, of course. But a few would. And these days, “a few” constitutes bipartisanship. It’s only the threshold of 60 that allows minority members to play these procedural shell games that give us the dysfunction we see constantly today.

A third argument you hear from some Democrats goes: Well, if we can pass A, B, and C with 51, can’t Republicans just undo them with 51 when they get power? The answer is yes, they can, in theory. But doing that isn’t nearly as easy as it sounds. Public opinion still matters in this country, and if public opinion is strongly for something, politicians are going to have a pretty hard time repealing it. How many years did Republicans scream about repealing Obamacare? But they never did it. Granted, it came close in 2017 in the Senate when John McCain cast the deciding “no” vote. But it failed. Repealing popular laws isn’t easy, even for ideological extremists.

Suppose the next Congress, both houses, pass a substantial minimum wage increase. And suppose Republicans hold the White House in 2029 and win back Congress. They’ll talk a lot about repealing the minimum wage. But a higher minimum wage is enormously popular. Will they really vote to take money out of people’s pockets? I say they probably won’t. And if they do, they’ll be committing political suicide.

A fourth and related argument is that with no filibuster, Republicans would be able to pass all kinds of reactionary things with 51 votes when they have power. Yes, I concede that this is true. And that would be pretty horrible in a lot of cases—awful “voter integrity” laws, Nazi-style laws about transgender people, who knows. But again, public opinion still matters. If these laws are unpopular, Republicans will pay the price in the next election. And Democrats can then not only undo them, but they can pass better laws that strengthen voting protections and trans rights. That’s democracy in action. Lex majoris partis.

On balance, the Democrats have a far broader legislative agenda than the Republicans do. So, on balance and over time, a reversion to simple majority rule will benefit the party with the fuller legislative agenda. Imagine a 2029 with a Democratic president, Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, and no filibuster threat in the Senate. If they wanted to, Democrats could pass law after law after law lifting wages and going after monopolists and price-gougers and expanding health care and greening the economy and all kinds of things. They could make FDR’s famous hundred days look like a trial run. The American people would be stunned at how well their government was functioning, and actually on their behalf. But with the filibuster in place, that future is completely unattainable.

4. Two Scenarios for the Next Congress

Two possible scenarios loom before us for the next Congress. Let’s consider them.

The Democrats campaigned on a few core promises: to stop funding the war; to reverse the Medicaid cuts; to restore the Obamacare subsidies; and to repeal Trump’s tariffs. There are many other bills the Democrats would like to pass—for example, some sort of Medicare expansion, now that that idea has Hakeem Jeffries’s blessing.

In fact, let’s imagine a bill that adds vision, hearing, and dental to Medicare and lowers the eligibility age to 60. That’s going to be a popular bill. But it’s also going to be an expensive bill; there’s no getting around that. Paying for it will probably involve some tax increases.

Imagine, then, that such a bill is introduced next year in both a no filibuster and a filibuster world. It passes the House in both scenarios. But in the Senate? It would almost surely pass in a no filibuster reality; Chuck Schumer (or Chris Van Hollen, whoever is in charge) could even let five nervous Democrats from red states, or four nervous red-staters plus Fetterman, vote “no,” and it would still pass. Plenty of cushion. Yes—Donald Trump would veto it. But the Democrats of both houses would have made a dramatic statement and fulfilled the broad campaign promise that they were committed to doing things to make people’s lives better.

In a filibuster reality, though, such a bill would have zero chance of getting through the Senate. Zero. This is not mere speculation, by the way. This, or something very like it, actually happened. In 2019, after the Democrats retook the House during Trump’s first term, House Democrats passed a bill sponsored by Frank Pallone of New Jersey that did not lower the eligibility age but sought to add vision, hearing, and dental benefits to Medicare, to be paid for by allowing the government to negotiate prescription drug prices. The vote in the House was 230–192, with just two Republicans joining 228 Democrats.

And the vote in the Senate? It’s a trick question. If you really know Capitol Hill, you know why: There was no vote in the Senate. Never came close. It was read twice and placed on the legislative calendar. And that was it. No doubt a large number of Democratic senators supported the bill and would have loved to see it pass. But the threat of a filibuster and the need for 60 votes made serious consideration of the bill completely impossible.

That is what’s going to happen with all of these Democratic bills. All of them. There might be a couple of exceptions. We know, for example, that Josh Hawley would probably back raising the minimum wage. Maybe Murkowski. But who else? And who’s going to be willing to be that sixtieth vote, ensuring that Donald Trump will take to Truth Social and call them a RINO and see to it that they face a well-financed primary challenge? Who’s going to be the sixtieth vote to restore Obamacare subsidies? Claw back the Medicaid cuts? Defund the war? Not happening, people.

Some of you by now are saying to yourselves, what about reconciliation? It’s true that Democrats can pass some things under the so-called “reconciliation” process, which is a way around the filibuster on certain spending and revenue matters. But reconciliation is a sloppy process—you sit around waiting for these arcane rulings from the Senate parliamentarian, it leads to big, omnibus bills that run to thousands of pages and that Republicans have found so easy to denounce; and reconciliation bills are temporary anyway. Democrats won’t have the political spine, or perhaps the political capital, to go to the reconciliation well too often. But if there were no filibuster, they could just … pass … bills.

5. So What Should the Democrats Do?

Before I answer that, I need to say: I’m just aghast that this isn’t being discussed by Democrats and liberals every day. It’s getting some oxygen. Van Hollen said recently that he is open to filibuster reform, calling it “anti-democratic,” but he didn’t commit to anything specific. A few senators are talking about it, a little. Jeff Merkley has been by far the best senator on this issue for years, trying to drag his stubborn colleagues toward actual democracy. With retiring Republican Steve Daines (and note that he’s retiring and has nothing to lose), Merkley has proposed a series of four reforms that would make it easier for bills with bipartisan support to go from committee to the floor. It would modify some cloture rules and eliminate it on certain matters. The reforms are good as far as they go, and it would be great to see the Senate adopt them, although it would take 67 votes to do so.

Others are talking about it in a far less constructive direction. On CNBC last week, Mark Warner said: “The filibuster saved our country’s bacon over the last couple years a number of times ... I don’t think we ought to get rid of the filibuster.” He’s referring to the fact that Trump leaned hard on Senate GOP leader John Thune to dump the filibuster for a few matters, like his beloved SAVE America Act. Thune held firm.

Warner’s remark, then, or the first half of it, is technically true. But what Warner is really saying here, although of course he didn’t and would never put it this way, is this: The filibuster stopped the Republicans from doing bad stuff, so therefore it ought to continue to exist so it can stop us from doing good stuff. He’s not recognizing that there’s any moral difference between a bill designed to block certain citizens from voting and bills designed to allow more people to afford health coverage or to help them pay for nursing care. It’s an unconscionable neutrality, in a country where people are hurting and angry that Washington is looking after billionaires but not them.

So what should the Democrats do? If they had real guts, they’d do this. At each new Congress, both House and Senate establish the rules under which they will operate. The House always adopts and votes on new rules. The Senate always calls itself a “continuing body” and rolls over the rules from the previous Senate.

If the Senate wanted to, it could say next January 3 that it’s no longer a “continuing body,” and as such it needs new rules. Then it could write those rules leaving the filibuster out. The passage of new rules requires only a simple majority. The filibuster would be dead.

That’s what the Democrats really ought to do. Short of that, they could at least reform the filibuster. They could simply lower the cloture threshold from 60 to 55 or 53. Tom Harkin once had a proposal to lower it in stages: 60 on the first cloture vote, 57 on a second, 54 on a third, and finally just 51 on a fourth. The idea is that it would give the minority time to make its case to the American public as the votes proceed, but that eventually, a simple majority could prevail.

Another idea is to force the minority to hold a “real” talking filibuster, of the Mr. Smith Goes to Washington sort. This wouldn’t guarantee that a filibuster couldn’t succeed, but it would force the minority to hold the floor for hours, attracting (mostly) negative media coverage as they read Green Eggs and Ham.

If I could wave a wand? I’d eliminate it, but short of that, Democrats could lower the threshold to 53 and make the minority hold the floor. This could conceivably be sold to recalcitrants like Warner as “reform” and not something so radical as elimination.

And finally, a key point: Some who support filibuster reform/elimination think Democrats should wait until 2028–29, when (hopefully) they’ll have an incoming Democratic president and actually be able to pass laws and not just pass bills that Trump will veto. I can see that argument. On the other hand, it can be argued that this is exactly the right time to do it because with a Republican in the White House, it won’t seem like a power grab. It can more easily be sold as an attempt to get the Senate moving again and not just a way to grease the skids for their legislative agenda.

6. Stop Sleepwalking

The filibuster debate must come out into the open, now. Democrats who support filibuster reform or elimination should be talking about this every day. Writers who agree with me need to write about it. Activists need to raise it on all the platforms at their disposal. Rank-and-file Democrats need to let their senators know that the status quo is not acceptable.

And every Democratic senator who does an MS NOW segment should not be allowed to leave until they have been asked: “Please tell me exactly how you’re going to get four Republicans votes for any of these things you campaigned on? And please don’t tell my viewers that you think Republicans will be willing to cooperate with you. My viewers have heard that song and dance way too many times. Tell us who the four votes are.”

I’ll conclude by asking you to imagine, again, two scenarios. It’s early 2028. In scenario one, the Democrats changed or eliminated the filibuster. They, in both House and Senate, passed a dozen bills designed to increase wages, expand health care, make workplaces fairer, help small farmers, make prescription drugs cheaper, and so on. And they restored Obamacare subsidies and Medicaid cuts. Trump has vetoed them all, so they haven’t become law. But the party has spoken loudly and acted clearly. Democrats have done what the people elected them to do. And they can go before the voters in 2028 and say: “We did what you elected us to do. These last two years prove only that we need a Democrat in the White House. You give us that, and we’ll pass every one of these bills all over again, and next time, they’ll become law.”

In scenario two, where they’ve done nothing about the filibuster, the House will have passed these bills, and with maybe one or two exceptions, every one of them will have died in the Senate. And by the way—Trump will have been spared the embarrassment of vetoing a dozen popular bills. In this scenario, the Republicans will be able to say: “See? The Democrats made you all these big promises. And they won control of both houses of Congress, and what did we see? The same old dysfunction. Those people can’t organize a two-car funeral. And all their big promises were a lie.” And the media would be constantly assailing the Democrats’ lack of “leadership” for failing to bring Republicans on board.

Chuck Schumer, which position would you rather be in? Mark Warner, did you not come to Washington to get things done for the people of Virginia and the United States? Democratic senators, are you seriously going to let this potentially amazing historical opportunity expire in the quicksand of a procedural oddity whose purpose through most of American history was to support slavery and quash civil rights?

The American people have just cried out to you: Donald Trump and the Republicans betrayed us. Please, please help us. Are you really prepared to tell them hey, I’d like to help, but preserving this one old rule is more important than improving your daily lives? If that’s really the Democrats’ answer, they will face the music in 2028. And they will deserve to.

items.title: JD Vance Lashes Out Over GOP Losses—and Reveals a Core MAGA Delusion
items.content_text:
If a person crosses the border into the United States illegally, is there any point at which they can develop a legitimate claim to belonging in our country? JD Vance thinks the answer to this question is no—period, full stop. Most Americans—even if only intuitively—appear to disagree. But rather than ask himself why that might be, he rejects that very possibility outright.

Now, as Republicans absorb the worst midterm wipeout in half a century, some of them are gently trying to talk Vance into taking a slightly more flexible position. It’s not going well.

Vance responded sharply last week when Kevin Sitt, the GOP governor of Oklahoma, suggested that Republicans should consider backing some form of bipartisan immigration reform to moderate a bit after their defeat. Vance replied:

I like Kevin, but what does “bipartisan immigration reform” mean? If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I’m all ears.

But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws.

It is morally and electorally disastrous.

Vance is wrong—on the substance, the morality, and the politics. This will be a big argument heading into 2028, so it’s worth offering a real reply.

Substance first: To Vance, reform that tightens enforcement is good while reform that gives longtime undocumented residents a path to legalization is bad. He’s for overhauling our visa system to make it harder for, say, big tech companies to bring in high-skill workers. He’d also strengthen requirements for companies to check applicants’ work authorization status before hiring them.

Good news, JD! One or both these enforcement ideas have been part of comprehensive immigration reform proposals going back over a decade. Such proposals have long included both tightened-up enforcement of exactly this sort and a path to legalization for certain groups of undocumented immigrants. This is the fundamental tradeoff that would get us out of our impasse, and everyone knows it. That, JD, is what bipartisan reform “means.”

The bipartisan Dignity Act, for instance, contains precisely that tradeoff. As Aaron Reichlin-Melnick explains, it would stiffen penalties against employers that fail to check work authorization and substantially boost border enforcement while providing paths to legalization for various undocumented groups. Vance could have the former and much more on enforcement tomorrow by accepting some version of the latter. All his post really means is that he won’t accept any such trade because no path to legalization is legitimate.

That is Vance’s central moral claim. To him, all such pathways are “amnesty” that reward “people who have broken our laws,” who he sees as irredeemable.

We liberals need to answer this frontally. Zack Beauchamp’s great new “Public Reason” project asks us to rehabilitate liberalism by redescribing how our principles should inform day-to-day politics. This is sorely needed on immigration, where the principled answer to Vance is almost never articulated, even though a whole literature exists to elaborate it.

The response goes as follows: Yes, undocumented immigrants violated our laws. But the controlling questions are: How serious a violation was this? Who was harmed? Does the original violation ever cease disqualifying a person from staying? In these deliberations, many factors should carry weight: the life circumstances of the actor, that person’s deeper intent, and their conduct over time after the offense.

All this is widely grasped in many areas, but on immigration, it’s particularly clear. A migrant’s reasons for coming—their prospects at home are dim or even dire—and their subsequent associations with the native-born pull heavily on us. Over time, as undocumented migrants demonstrate good intentions toward Americans and contribute positively to our economies and communities, we see them as gradually developing a conditional claim to belonging.

While other arguments can be invoked here—freedom of movement, global justice, the nation’s need for more people—the above, I believe, is the ethical argument that resonates intuitively with most people.

Take noted moral philosopher Joe Rogan. He’s expressing a version of those claims when he says that it’s “not a good thing to snatch people out of their fucking taco stand that have been in the country for 20 years—and are nice, good people that are beloved by the community—but just don’t have the right paperwork.”

In this telling, the original violation becomes understood as exceptionally low-harm and low-stakes. It then transforms itself into a net positive for our country.

Vance cannot grasp how people might react this way, because he sees illegal entry as a special kind of harm. It’s a wound delivered to his conception of the identity of the American volk. As Vance himself has suggested, the spiritual health of the nation depends on people’s lines of heritage and blood reaching as deep into the American past as possible, ideally into the generations of nineteenth century settlers who braved the foggy Appalachian frontier or were tested by the trials of the Civil War.

But this schema collapses under minimal scrutiny. It can’t explain where the waves of immigrants who arrived at the turn of the twentieth century—and after the 1965 end to racial immigration quotas—rank on his Hierarchy of Belonging. It’s not clear if Vance believes—as Stephen Miller apparently does—that migrants whose ancestral past originated outside the enchanted “West,” in places like Africa, the Middle East, and the indigenous Americas, are intrinsically unfit to become U.S. citizens. But they’re plainly lower on his imagined hierarchy.

None of it survives the light of American history or basic logic, and it’s a terrible basis for tackling the problem of the undocumented. In the paramilitary Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids—which are routinely depicted in government communications with just this sort of rapturous ethnonationalist fervor—we’re now seeing this worldview translated into policy. It hasn’t fulfilled Vance’s promise of jobs for the native-born, instead leading to vicious social conflict and blood running in U.S. streets.

Of course, Vance might object to legalization on other grounds. He might say there’s no obvious way to determine what amount of time here should negate the original illegal border-crossing. The answer to this is that we make this decision democratically. Our elected representatives can set what conditions various undocumented populations must meet to live and work in our country, factoring in the broader national interest in doing so.

Which leads, finally, to Vance’s political argument. Vance claims passing comprehensive reform would be “electorally disastrous.” Vance might mean it would deflate the MAGA movement’s hard-core ethnonationalist base. But to the degree he’s also saying the broader American mainstream will reject “amnesty” for all illegal border crossers, this is obviously false.

The polling is consistent: No matter how the question is asked, solid majorities support paths to legalization for people who meet certain conditions. That last bit is critical: Most Americans grasp that the criteria built into such proposals—eligibility and language requirements, law enforcement check-ins—constitute reasonable hurdles given the original offense and the offender’s subsequent conduct.

Post-liberals like Vance love to tell liberals that their understanding of “human nature” is fatally unrealistic. But in the real world, most people’s instinctual grasp of this morally messy situation doesn’t prove nearly as rigid as Vance’s does. We understand that if people come illegally, it’s because we make it absurdly difficult to come legally. We acknowledge we might have done the same. We know our good fortune in being born American—and the bad luck of those seeking refuge here—is largely arbitrary.

Vance would reject that idea too. A Catholic convert with Christian nationalist inclinations, he likely believes his own lineage reaching deep into the misty Kentucky mountains was not arbitrary—it was providentially ordained. To people who think this way, we can only reply: That can’t be the basis for solving the undocumented problem in a secular liberal democracy, and regardless, most Americans want it solved our way.

Vance’s core conundrum is this: Majorities of Americans simply don’t see the offense of entering and living here illegally as a permanently disqualifying one. That might be distressing for those who see it as an act of profound violence against mystically conjured visions of the American nation’s true essence. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t true.

items.title: How Democrats Can Actually Deliver on Affordability
items.content_text:
If there’s one thing Democrats can agree on, it’s that affordability is important. Exit polling showed that the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how nearly 90 percent of voters cast their ballots for the next Congress. More than 8 in 10 voters in this year’s midterms were “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities, and health care.

What exactly “affordability” means, however—and how Democrats can deliver it—is less obvious. While Democrats will take control of both houses of Congress next year, their options for actually bringing down costs are somewhat limited. It could be especially challenging to do so in ways that voters will feel by November 2028. So long as Trump is in the White House, he can still veto Congressional attempts to reassert legislative control over tariffs or claw back the administration’s costly and chaotic trade policies. The same will likely be true of attempts to end the war in Iran—another top concern that’s helped drive up prices for everything from food to heating oil.

What, then, are Democrats to do? There may be some areas for bipartisan cooperation on certain bills, and Democrats will have more leverage over must-pass legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act. But the core of the party’s near-term agenda is likely to flow through its leadership of House and Senate committees. Here, aside from being able to reject certain White House staffing decisions, Democrats will take on oversight powers that allow them to issue subpoenas to government officials and corporate executives. With agenda-setting power and beefed-up staffing, they can initiate investigations, make Cabinet officials and CEOs alike testify before Congress, and compel federal agencies and Fortune 500 companies to produce reams of documents that wouldn’t otherwise be available to the public.

These privileges are nothing to sneeze at. But Democrats are nonetheless in a slightly awkward position. Voters trust them to “handle the economy” more than Republicans by nearly 10 points, according to midterms exit polling. But as the party looks ahead to a presidential election where the economy is likely to be just as important—when it will need to defend its Congressional majorities too—it will somehow need to maintain its credibility on economic issues while having relatively little control over them. Complicating matters is the fact that Trump could still do a lot of damage in his remaining two years, potentially leaving Democrats to inherit an economy that’s far worse off in 2029. And whether there’s an economic downturn or not, wealth inequality is likely to continue apace. Just this week, Anthropic’s initial public offering made roughly 5,300 people as wealthy as the poorest 45 million U.S. households—a third of the country. As of Thursday, Anthropic’s seven co-founders were worth a staggering $163 billion. Against a backdrop of extreme uncertainty and ballooning inequality, how can Democrats help voters trust them to make their lives more affordable—and grant them the kinds of majorities needed to overhaul the structures that keep the economy so unequal?

While the kinds of changes Democrats can make over the next two years are relatively small-scale, they can still take on big targets. The Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive think tank, is urging Democrats to make creative use of the powers they will have. Shortly after the election, reports emerged that the group had circulated a 181-page document on Capitol Hill outlining an extensive list of prospective hearing topics and investigation targets in industries ranging from health care and energy to retail, food, and insurance. Not long after, calls started pouring in. “We’ve gotten a lot of outreach from K Street, and inquiries from lobbyists who are looking to staff up and get prepared,” said Alex Jacquez, Groundwork’s senior vice president.

Where the party directs that scrutiny will matter a lot. Groundwork conducted focus groups late last summer about Congress’s oversight powers, gathering opinions from four particular groups: voters who had attended or were likely to attend a No Kings protests; “Gettable Former Democrats,” who used to support Democrats and don’t strongly identify with Republicans; battleground swing state voters who aren’t strong partisans; and multiracial working-class voters without college degrees, in a low-to-moderate income bracket. They found that working class voters and “gettable” former Democrats reacted most positively to Congress prioritizing investigations into corporate greed. Such a focus helped “overcome voters’ skepticism that Democrats are more focused on partisan warfare than on the problems of everyday Americans,” Groundwork writes, and suspicions that both parties are corrupt. Focus group participants were skeptical that oversight investigations would make any sort of difference in their lives, bolstering the case for Democrats to prioritize areas where applying pressure—for things like corruption, price gouging and wage theft—could yield real results. Voters were particularly eager to see investigations into Big Tech, drug manufacturers, health care, and oil and gas companies.

By using their oversight powers effectively, Democrats can speak to voters’ concerns and secure tangible relief. “This is not the place you’re likely to see more structural reforms,” Jacquez said. “But there is a good history of congressional oversight leading to real material changes in corporate behavior.”

As recently as 2024, for instance, the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions requested that four of the country’s biggest manufacturers of inhalers hand over documents related to how they set prices for those products. Sufferers of asthma and other respiratory conditions need to purchase inhalers monthly, which at the time could range in price from between $200 and $600 apiece. In the U.S., GlaxoSmithKline charged roughly $319 for the asthma medication Advair HFA; in the United Kingdom, it charged the equivalent of just $26 for the same inhaler. Before pricing documents were released to the public, three of the four targeted manufacturers, including GlaxoSmithKline, agreed to cap inhaler prices at $35 a month.

Repeating those kinds of wins would likely be the result of public pressure rather than the threat of federal civil or criminal charges, which would still need to be referred to Trump’s Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice. At the state level, though, attorneys general could piggyback on investigations, and potentially even delist companies that are legally domiciled in their jurisdictions. Newly elected Democratic majorities at public utility regulators in Georgia and Arizona could also ramp up pressure on utilities’ ability to pass grid-connected data centers’ mounting power costs onto customers. For congressional Democrats, oversight actions that result in real-world cost reductions—however small-scale—can offer proof of concept that voters should continue to trust them more than Republicans to manage the economy.

As Jacquez is clear to point out, taking on the structural causes of high prices will require more sweeping changes. “Affordability is not just certain prices of consumer goods going up,” said Melanie Brusseler, U.S. Program Director for the economics think tank Common Wealth. Some of the biggest pain points, she adds—for essentials like housing, childcare and health care—“are in places where the scale of the costs are so systemic to the organization of those sectors that you really need a comprehensive reorganization.”

Health care, for example—the economy’s largest sector, responsible for a sixth of GDP and one in seven jobs—is composed of everything from drug and device manufacturing to home health aides, hospitals, and insurance. Making health care more affordable is hardly as simple as finding examples of price gouging by drug manufacturers, which can certainly help but won’t fix the many perverse incentives baked into a system where supply and demand alike are organized around private profitability. Common Wealth has argued for reimagining the state’s role in the production and provision of such essential goods and services, where it already offers considerable support to private sector providers via favorable tax treatment, regulatory relief and subsidization. That doesn’t mean eliminating private sector involvement in those sectors so much as recognizing its limits, and the essential role governments tend to play in directing investment toward essential physical and social infrastructure that also happens to be unprofitable.

“Affordability and economic security do not depend on prices alone,” economist Isabella Weber likewise writes in her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. “An economy for the common people requires a floor under the living conditions of all. Affordable essentials, living wages, and a full employment economy mean that fewer people become dependent on social benefits, but a strong safety net is there to ensure dignity for all. But it also requires a ceiling to limit extreme wealth, extreme profits, and corporate power—and the individual overuse of our collective resources.

Democrats’ longer-term challenge isn’t just to bring down Trump-era prices hikes, but to put forward a compelling vision for macroeconomic management that ensures life’s essentials are never out of reach. That’ll almost certainly mean taking on corporate interests, which is something the 120th Congress can start doing on day one.

items.title: America Promised AIDS Relief. Then Abandoned Millions of People.
items.content_text:
On the first day of his second term as president, Donald Trump effectively turned off medical care for tens of millions of people living with HIV around the globe. That day, January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order halting all U.S. foreign aid for 90 days. Among the initiatives affected by the pause was the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, known as PEPFAR, a decades-old program that was supporting some 20 million people with HIV, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa, home to roughly two-thirds of those living with the virus worldwide.

The repercussions were immediate. Medical providers across Africa received stop-work orders from the U.S. government. Warnings blared from radio stations in central Uganda, the journalist Andrew Green reported, informing listeners that HIV treatments would shut down for the 90-day “pause” that Trump demanded. One man who heard this announcement, Juma Bwanika, immediately started rationing his antiretroviral medication. “Ever since this order from Trump,” he told Green, “I am seeing death near me.”

Confusion reigned. In the face of outrage and outcry, the administration granted PEPFAR a waiver that allowed it to resume certain “lifesaving” services, but it was not initially clear which services qualified, and that muddle, combined with broader cuts across the U.S. government, led some African HIV care providers to tell the press that “the waiver was meaningless and services remained suspended.” In the months that followed, many of those relying on PEPFAR were able to maintain access to medicine, but many of the on-the-ground testing, treatment, and prevention efforts disappeared. A study from mid-2026 estimated that 1,700 HIV treatment sites had shut down due to cuts or delays in funding. As Green reported, the U.S. government is negotiating new agreements with African countries to sharply reduce U.S. commitments; some of these agreements even tie U.S. funding to access to African mineral rights. PEPFAR remains at risk of running out of money. And some observers have estimated that almost 160,000 adults and 17,000 children died as a result of just the first year of PEPFAR cuts.

Amid this roiling catastrophe, John Donnelly’s new book, Lifeline: The Story of PEPFAR, the Greatest Humanitarian Initiative of Our Time, provides a clear accounting of all that’s been needlessly forsaken. Over nearly a quarter-century, PEPFAR saved some 26 million lives, prevented eight million HIV transmissions in utero, and provided testing for over 80 million people. In an age of austerity and mounting xenophobia, the U.S. government spent more than $120 billion to fight AIDS around the world, with most of that money going toward health care in Africa. “No program in the history of US foreign assistance compares with PEPFAR’s impact,” Donnelly writes.

Donnelly, who spent many years covering the HIV/AIDS crisis in Africa for The Boston Globe before decamping to advise the president of the World Bank, brings considerable authority to the project. He has ample access to George W. Bush, the former president’s top advisers, and many of PEPFAR’s architects in the United States and abroad and uses it to assemble a valuable record of the creation and rollout of PEPFAR. He plainly hopes the book will provide a model for future interventions—the story of PEPFAR “should be a master class in how countries confront future global crises,” he writes in the introduction—and inspire future policymakers.

Some observers have estimated that almost 160,000 adults and 17,000 children died as a result of just the first year of pepfar cuts

Yet the model that Lifeline offers is an imperfect one. Donnelly is far too sympathetic to his sources, and far too invested in telling an upbeat story, to provide the kind of critical account that might actually be useful to those in power in a post-DOGE, post-Trump moment—when the United States will need to reformulate a foreign policy for a world of deepening inequities and proliferating nationalisms. To understand how to engage in such a world, and how to do so in a manner that actually reduces harm, requires an understanding of subjects Donnelly doesn’t address, such as how U.S. actions in Africa created the conditions that demanded an emergency humanitarian response, and how the flaws in that humanitarian response left PEPFAR open to such a swift obliteration by the Trump administration.


In 1996, after well over a decade of unchecked suffering, the first effective AIDS medications became widely available. For most infected Africans, however, they were inaccessible or far too expensive. “Everyone seemed to be celebrating,” Donnelly recounts early in Lifeline, “but no one was talking about what it meant for the continent that was home to 70 percent of the world’s HIV/AIDS infections.” Over the next few years, patients in wealthy countries experienced miraculous improvements (a phenomenon so striking it came to be called the “Lazarus effect”), while the epidemic deepened in much of the developing world, in part because major pharmaceutical companies spent years fighting African efforts to import cheaper, generic versions of the drugs. “The disease has built up significant momentum,” a U.S. government report noted in 2002, to the point that its continued spread risked turning major hot spots like Nigeria and Ethiopia into “seriously weakened states.”

Following George W. Bush’s ascent to the presidency at the start of the millennium, most knowledgeable observers “believed that the new administration would pay little attention to AIDS in Africa,” Donnelly writes. But Bush would surprise them. Slowly, tentatively, he would direct a handful of advisers (including Anthony Fauci) to formulate an ambitious plan to combat AIDS in Africa. The president’s motivations were both humanitarian and realpolitik. In Donnelly’s telling, Bush was genuinely moved by the plight of those with AIDS, but he also felt “that a war on terror also must include some type of humanitarian response in areas of the world where Al Qaeda and other terror groups were actively recruiting members.” If the United States were seen as a benevolent source of aid, the thinking went, potential recruits might be less likely to want to attack it.

For much of 2002, Bush’s advisers worked in secret to draw up a road map for bringing treatment to some of the remotest parts of the African continent. Its price tag was a staggering $15 billion. Bush revealed the proposal in his 2003 State of the Union, calling the plan “a work of mercy.” An obliging Congress allotted the requested funding, and the money spigot began to open across Africa. Before PEPFAR, Donnelly observes, the nation of Rwanda had just eight treatment sites; by the end of 2005, it had 103 sites, as well as a sophisticated recordkeeping system employing mobile phones. Millions of people who would otherwise have met brutal deaths are instead alive today.

Donnelly’s admiration for PEPFAR and all that it accomplished is eminently understandable. But his book is a remarkably uncritical one. His goal, it seems, was to craft a straightforwardly heroic narrative, to provide his readers with a model that, he notes, was enacted with “bipartisan support,” under the watch of a reasonable, self-described “compassionate” conservative Republican. To fashion such a narrative, however, Donnelly had to overlook a lot.

For instance, the book is positively wistful for a time when the two parties could work together. Readers learn that Bobby Shriver, a liberal attorney (and Kennedy scion) tasked with getting congressional Democrats to support Bush’s plan, started finding his calls with conservative White House operative Karl Rove “enjoyable” as the two laughed together. Readers encounter Republican senatorial staffers calling more conservative legislators “the crazies” and working with the Democrats to obtain more funding for PEPFAR over the objections of the craziest.

But this tale of bipartisanship is carefully constructed to minimize or outright elide information that might diminish its feel-good quality. While Donnelly writes that Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist reacted to the surprise news of the PEPFAR proposal “with grace and appreciation” and then spends pages documenting Frist’s efforts to guide the PEPFAR funding bill through the Senate, he provides no information on the reaction or actions of the speaker of the House, who was also instrumental in obtaining the funding. Such silence is puzzling—until, that is, one recalls that the speaker at the time was the late Dennis Hastert, who in 2016 was sent to prison for illegal hush payments made to boys he had sexually abused. Had Donnelly so much as mentioned his name (Lifeline does not), this might have complicated the safely digestible story of good people doing good things that he set out to tell.

In fact, virtually every star in the early-2000s political firmament receives a flattering shout-out, from Condoleezza Rice to Jesse Helms to White House adviser Jay Lefkowitz (revealed only in an afterword to be “best known for representing sex offender Jeffrey Epstein,” though he “also took on many pro bono cases”). So much of Lifeline is about the hard work and dedication of federal officials, with dozens and dozens of pages recounting the quotidian details of their meetings and evolving proposals, occasionally enriched with long, earnest conversations, apparently sourced solely from the recollections of the participants decades after the fact.

Yet no figure in Lifeline is portrayed as favorably, or as selectively, as George W. Bush. Almost every chapter contains one luminary or another praising the former president’s acumen or empathy. The pioneering Ugandan physician Peter Mugyenyi, for instance, declares that most “people are insensitive to Africans’ hurt. President Bush was not.” Donnelly himself concludes that “the global AIDS plan had become, against all odds, Bush’s one legacy that would rise above everything else in his eight years in office.” This is, at least, a debatable proposition, considering Bush is also the architect of the modern surveillance state and of the global war on terrorism. But readers learn little of those initiatives. Instead, they encounter anecdotes of Bush being gracious to a gay staffer, and several pages devoted to Bush’s daughter, Barbara, leaving her charmed life to take an internship at a South African AIDS ward. Donnelly gives Bush the last word, as the former president laments that “Americans ought to be proud of what we have done.”

Donnelly also does Bush the favor of largely adopting his preferred framing of PEPFAR and the causes of its success. Explaining why Bush ultimately decided that the United States should fund its own program instead of just allotting the funds to the United Nations’ efforts, Donnelly uncritically reproduces Bush’s view that the United Nations lacked accountability, that it couldn’t guarantee results. (In fact, since 2002, the U.N. “Global Fund” has helped prevent tens of millions of deaths due to HIV, malaria, and tuberculosis, though it can be difficult to separate the lives saved by the Global Fund from those saved by PEPFAR.) Similarly, Donnelly relays the critique by Bush’s staff that the U.S. Agency for International Development, or USAID, was “a huge bureaucracy that focused more on spending money than tracking outcomes.” (The second Trump administration apparently agreed, as it effectively destroyed USAID.) By contrast, PEPFAR existed outside of the established structures of government and gathered “more data than any development program in history.” In emphasizing the program’s dynamism, Donnelly even adopts the idiom of the tech industry, referring to PEPFAR—a governmental initiative—as a “billion-dollar start-up,” “a start-up that could avoid the traps of the bureaucracy,” and “a unicorn.”

Tellingly, Donnelly overlooks some of the strongest criticisms of PEPFAR. While he notes that some of his subjects disagreed with Bush’s refusal to allow other countries to provide funding for PEPFAR, or to simply devote the billions allotted for the U.S.-only effort to the U.N. AIDS fund instead, Donnelly appears unaware that there is an entire body of literature critiquing PEPFAR’s actual work over the past several decades. For instance, the academic Wiebe Nauta has argued that the U.S. approach placed far too much emphasis on addressing African sexual behavior (e.g., pushing monogamy and abstinence) while overlooking structural forces like inequality or poverty. More recently, epidemiologist Alison Wiyeh and her co-authors asked “why, after 21 years of PEPFAR support and over $120 billion in investment, PEPFAR-funded countries remain reliant on external assistance, lacking a clear framework for sustainable, country-led HIV/AIDS responses,” and concluded that PEPFAR’s “vertical, disease-specific approach” has created “structurally fragile health programs” that cannot function independently or without outside support.

Indeed, one study of Mozambique noted that PEPFAR funding came to nearly equal the budget of the country’s health ministry and did result in a “real, measurable impact on the HIV epidemic,” but “health system fundamentals and basic coverage have barely changed.” Over half of Mozambicans still have to walk over an hour to reach a health care facility, and the proportion of such facilities per capita actually declined even as the PEPFAR coffers stayed open.

Such critiques, even though difficult to read about a program that has unquestionably improved millions of lives, are far more illuminating than Donnelly’s careful story of mercy, pluck, and good intentions. Lifeline is rich with important and interesting details, but it is markedly incurious—about PEPFAR’s limitations, about the flaws of many of its architects, and about the globally unequal burden of AIDS that PEPFAR was created to address.


Among the subtlest but most important of Donnelly’s omissions is any consideration of why a program like ­PEPFAR was necessary in the first place. “At first glance, it seems merely an accident of fate that people living in poor countries are both more likely to get HIV and less likely to have access to the medicines that make living with HIV possible,” the sociologist Carol Heimer has written. “Yet the two are causally connected, and the poor South’s relation to the rich North is part and parcel of that connection.” In other words, the United States and the other wealthy countries sending money to Africa are not merely firefighters bringing desperately needed water to a near-uncontrollable blaze. They are also the arsonists.

To understand such a statement requires a review of history wholly absent from Lifeline. It is quite likely that simian immunodeficiency virus, or SIV—the chimpanzee retrovirus that is the immediate evolutionary precursor to human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV—had been periodically jumping from apes to humans in Central Africa for hundreds or even thousands of years. But until the mid-twentieth century, such transmissions never spread far enough to become an epidemic, much less a global one.

What changed, according to a wide range of scholars (notably the epidemiologist Jacques Pépin), was the colonization of Africa by Western powers like France and Belgium. In short, zoonotic transmissions that in earlier years would have remained isolated now had the chance to reach many more people, as the forced labor imposed by colonial viceroys led huge numbers of Africans to migrate to cities; the establishment of labor camps (and tacit encouragement of sex work at these camps) and the imposition of Western public health campaigns (especially vaccination drives carried out with unsterilized needles) likewise contributed to viral spread. By the time the medical authorities noticed a “rare cancer” afflicting gay men in New York and California in 1981, the virus had long since circulated far, far beyond its point of emergence in southeastern Cameroon.

In the decades that followed, HIV cases rose all around the world, but nowhere more sharply than in sub-Saharan Africa. Once again, this dynamic is inseparable from the role of powerful actors far outside Africa. As early as 1991, the researchers David Sanders and Abdulrahman Sambo noted that budget cuts and other austerity measures imposed on African countries in the 1980s at the behest of U.S.-backed institutions like the International Monetary Fund “aggravate the transmission, spread and control of HIV infection in Africa in two major ways: directly by increasing the population at risk through increased urban migration, poverty, women’s powerlessness and prostitution, and indirectly through a decrease in health care provision.”

Donnelly’s account, moving though it often is, is shorn of this context. To his credit, he devotes much of Lifeline to the country of Uganda, giving voices and names to African actors (a narrative choice that many of the epidemic’s chroniclers fail to make), but at no point do readers learn, say, how economic policies created by the U.S. Treasury Department, the IMF, and the World Bank “exacerbated Uganda’s HIV crisis by accelerating the collapse of the coffee sector, Uganda’s largest industry and its primary source of waged labor for poor women,” in the words of the anthropologist Erin V. Moore and several co-authors. Deprived of previously reliable coffee jobs, many women had little choice but to undertake various forms of transactional sex just as the HIV epidemic was emerging across the country.

Nor do readers learn of the role of George W. Bush in entrenching poverty in Africa—in rendering the continent vulnerable to unchecked epidemics. During his presidency, Bush declined to address the crippling debt burdening many African nations or the place of these nations at the extractive end of global supply chains. Instead, he aggressively pushed African countries to open their economies to the global market, even as his administration engaged in economic protectionism at home. The effects for millions of Africans were stark. For instance, the Bush administration’s subsidization of U.S. cotton producers had massive impacts on the global cotton industry, costing West Africa some $191 million. While one can certainly contest such an interpretation of the consequences of Bush-era economic initiatives, Donnelly doesn’t engage with it at all.

To be sure, documenting the consequences of colonialism and neocolonialism was not Donnelly’s project. But its absence is, in a sense, perverse—like a book praising the charity of the English toward the famine-stricken Irish without acknowledging the vital English role in rendering Ireland vulnerable to the great potato famine in the first place. Without such context, a history is necessarily incomplete.

More importantly, such a history can never be a usable one. How do we prevent the next epidemic? How do we ameliorate the present one? The answer does not lie in a paean to a political order that is dead and gone—and that was complicit in much of the suffering anyway. The task instead is to fight for a political order that refuses to countenance the poverty, inequality, and exploitation that transform disease into disaster.

items.title: Trump Accidentally Reveals How Putin Manipulates Him in Epic Self-Own
items.content_text: Donald Trump’s “summit” with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping has been widely pilloried for accomplishing nothing. But Trump made things worse in talking to reporters. In a strange ramble, he basically admitted straight out that Putin’s treatment of him during the Russia scandal mattered far more to him than how Putin’s policies impact our national interest. In another moment, he buffoonishly claimed that Putin privately assured him he would have never invaded Ukraine with Trump as president. Of course not, Donald, you are so strong! All this unwittingly lays bare how Putin has played on Trump’s megalomania for years to get Trump to be a pliable tool. We unraveled what really happened at the “summit” with foreign policy expert Elizabeth Saunders. She explains how Putin and Xi’s manipulation of Trump boosts authoritarianism abroad, what’s really driving the two leaders, how lame-duck Trump can still do tremendous international damage, and how Democrats can limit it. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: “Dumbass” RFK Jr. Rescued Measles From Obscurity. What Horror Is Next?
items.content_text:
“You dumbass, your thing can’t be the measles! That can’t be your project: giving people the measles.” Thus quipped Saturday Night Live host John Mulaney, who used the back half of his monologue last weekend to savagely fillet Trump’s health and human services secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Naturally, the bit riled up plenty of conservative commentators, for whom the sugar high of previous SNL host Shane Gillis referring to women who exercise as “whores” has apparently worn off, and soured them on stand-up comedy anew. Would that they might be angrier at the news that landed Kennedy in the proverbial hot seat. As The Wall Street Journal reported last Friday, the Trump administration notched another historic achievement when the United States lost the measles-elimination status it obtained in 2000—”a stunning reversal for a nation that has kept the vaccine-preventable disease at bay for decades.” It’s kind of axiomatic: If you don’t want Saturday Night Live to stunt on you for spreading measles, don’t spread the measles.

This news may have flown under the radar because nothing much was flying above the radar at the time: The measles news was overshadowed by the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop that left travelers stranded across the country. Well, not everyone was grounded: Department of Homeland Security head and public communications genius Markwayne Mullin told the nation that the ground stop was not “another 9/11” and then hopped a private jet to Baton Rouge to watch Lane Kiffin, the Bari Weiss of college football coaches, fumble away another LSU victory against the University of Texas. No one else in the Trump administration covered themselves in glory that weekend, as various members of his inner circle and Cabinet blamed the snafu on everything from copper wire to Joe Biden to trans people. The headline of the Drudge Report on Monday was “USA BROKEN.”

Our failings on the transportation front are in part down to the fact that the Department of Transportation is run by C-list reality-television entity Sean Duffy, who is more interested in telling people how to dress on planes than in making sure his department is adequately staffed to prevent those planes from crashing. But the role that Kennedy has played in “USA BROKEN” has been decidedly dogged and a lot more hands-on. Unlike Duffy, Kennedy has been clocked in, mainly to systematically cripple the nation’s ability to respond to measles cases, which as of Tuesday have “surged to more than 7,700 nationwide, with 13 deaths, the highest totals for both in nearly four decades.”

Those figures come from Tuesday’s blockbuster Reuters report detailing the extent to which Trump and Kennedy have essentially encouraged the spread of measles. Prior to Kennedy’s misrule, Reuters reports, the federal government used to respond to such outbreaks with a robust approach that combined vaccine education and the mobilization of experts to affected areas. Now, they report, officials have stopped promoting immunization and aren’t showing up to help. And it’s Kennedy’s quack hands on the rudder that are largely to blame.

The Reuters report is based on a comprehensive analysis of public health data from “13 states and New York City.” Overall, it confirms a “significant vaccination pullback for younger children under Kennedy’s watch in 2025 than during the pandemic and in any year since then.” Infectious disease experts who reviewed the report’s findings were alarmed, telling Reuters that “even small declines in vaccination rates can quickly translate into many more infections.” Anne Schuchat, who served as the principal deputy director of the CDC during Trump’s first presidential foray, said that “the absence of federal leadership in measles outbreaks” has been “particularly destructive,” and that it will “take years to reverse the public-health damage.” She added, “The worst is probably ahead of us.”

While Secretary of “War” Pete Hegseth has lately been the central figure in the postelection impeachment dramas, many have been calling for Kennedy’s head, as well. The National Nurses Union is one of the loudest voices in the fray, and the administration’s asleep-at-the-switch posture on the measles is the biggest reason why. STAT News columnist Paul Knoepfler concurs: The election of so many doctors and scientists to office makes these election results a “biomedical blue wave”—and with it comes a “unique opportunity” to send Kennedy packing. Chris Geidner, the writer of the LawDork newsletter, helpfully suggests that “each article of impeachment [should] be the name of every measles death.”

Impeachment is said to be on the radar for Democrats in the ascendence, according to a recent report for PBS News—but there is something of a hiccup as Democrats also, for reasons I cannot fathom, are trying to “court” members of the MAHA movement. Personally, I think anyone affiliated with this right-wing woo-wooery should either convert to the rational world or remain an albatross around the necks of the GOP. However, according to PBS, “members of the MAHA movement said they’re eager to work with Democrats to pass legislation on shared interests, like regulating pesticides and making school lunches healthier.”

Give unto me a break. Democrats should simply do both those things and mitigate Kennedy’s damage by any means necessary. And while a successful impeachment of Kennedy raises serious concern about who would succeed him—no Trump administration replacement is ever better than their predecessor—Democrats will have a 56-senator firewall against the confirmation of further whackadoos. (Though admittedly, one of those 56 will be the whackadoo-adjacent John Fetterman.)

The one thing we know for certain about the future is that there are dark days ahead. The ascension of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff will, multiple reports suggest, reinvigorate Kennedy’s authority and the MAHA movement. “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration,” Kennedy posted on X. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” Unleashing the Kraken probably puts Democrats on the path to another blue wave in two years’ time, sure. But it also means that Kennedy is going to have a lot more time and opportunity to do what he does best: kill people.

This article first appeared in Power Mad, a weekly TNR newsletter authored by deputy editor Jason Linkins. Sign up here.

items.title: “Rude”: Trump Snaps at Woman Reporter Who Dared to Ask Question
items.content_text:
The president tore into an NBC reporter after a rambling press conference Friday, lashing out at the woman for trying to ask a question as he heaped praise onto White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

“I’m going to end it on Stephen, he’s really, he deserves it because forget about his little statement that he made right now, he covered a lot of territory, he’s been with me a long time he’s really a talent,” Trump swooned. “He’s got a big heart. A lot of people think he doesn’t, they think he’s hard on immigration, hard on this—he’s got a tremendous heart.”

But a question from NBC News White House correspondent Monica Alba on the matter was apparently enough to immediately send Trump over the edge.

“Please, come on,” Trump said, incredulously motioning towards the reporter. “Who are you with? Who are you with?”

“I’m with NBC, sir,” Alba said.

“You are really a rude person,” Trump retorted.

The president didn’t handle it much better when Alba pointed out that her question—at a press conference, no less—was relevant to the topic at hand.

“Well you’re talking about immigration, sir,” she said.

“I’m not talking to you,” Trump spat back. “You shouldn’t be in the front row. You should be in the back row.”

Not long afterward, the White House’s Rapid Response account on X slammed Alba as a “VERY rude Fake News loser from NBC.”

“These people truly have no shame,” the account posted. “It’s disgusting how they act in the presence of the President of the United States.”

But if Trump can’t handle the heat, then he should probably get out of the kitchen, as this is far from the first time that Trump has erupted at a woman journalist. Last year, Trump abruptly ended a line of questioning about the Epstein files by barking at a female Bloomberg News reporter, “Quiet! Quiet, piggy.” Then in February, Trump similarly skewered CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins for bringing up Jeffrey Epstein’s myriad victims, declaring that she was the “worst reporter” and doesn’t smile enough.

Recently, Trump has wagged his finger at ABC News’s Rachel Scott, repeatedly interrupted a female reporter during an Oval Office announcement, and verbally attacked CBS News’s Nancy Cordes and CNN’s Kristen Holmes. Just this week, Trump torched Alba’s colleague, NBC News reporter Yamiche Alcindor, calling her “pathetic” and talentless for asking about the nationwide FAA ground stop.

items.title: Did Pete Hegseth Use Weird Internet Searches to Decide Who to Promote?
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth blocked promotions for DOD officers who’d publicly supported figures or policies caught in the crossfire of his pointless culture wars. Now, Senate Democrats want him to explain himself.

A senior Pentagon official told MS NOW that Hegseth has directed Pentagon workers to conduct internet searches on officials recommended for promotion to one- or two- star ranks, in order to see if they’d supported policies such as efforts to promote Covid-19 vaccines, participation in diversity equity, and inclusion events, or the U.S withdrawal from Afghanistan.

Pentagon staffers were also instructed to see if officers had supported General Mark Milley, the former chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who described Donald Trump as a “fascist” and a “wannabe dictator.”

Those internet searches prevented the promotion of 17 officers, the senior official said. All of the women and people of color who were selected for promotion, save for one, were also withheld. This is not the first report that Hegseth has moved to block or delay the promotion of members of marginalized groups.

Hegseth personally intervened to block the promotion of several senior Navy officers, including at least two female officers and two Black male officers, four current and former defense officials revealed in June. He did the same thing to Army officers in March, and has reportedly thwarted the advancements of more than one dozen female and Black officers across the Army, Air Force, Navy, and the Marines.

In a letter obtained by MS NOW Friday, Senator Mark Kelly demanded that Hegseth explain why he blocked perfectly capable officers from ascending through the ranks.

“It is particularly troubling that officers may be penalized for faithfully implementing lawful policies and directives issued by previous administrations,” Kelly wrote. “This sends a dangerous message that servicemembers’ careers depend on whether their past service aligns with the political preferences of the current administration, rather than their performance, judgment, and leadership.”
