items.title: White House Was Reportedly Blindsided By Iowa's Lead Explosives, And Now Someone At The Army May Pay
items.content_text:
White House Was Reportedly Blindsided By Iowa's Lead Explosives, And Now Someone At The Army May Pay

The Army's detonation of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, went off Wednesday morning with no airborne lead picked up by any of the EPA's monitors, and by evening officials had lifted the shelter-in-place order for everyone within 20 miles. Inside the Trump administration, the relief has already turned into a hunt for who let it get that far.

The White House was blindsided by the danger at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and is now searching for accountability, sources told CBS News on Wednesday. Trump was relieved by the result but furious with how the Army handled the matter in the months before, three sources told the network, and there have been internal conversations about the role of Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's chief of staff. 

Other officials pushed back, arguing that the dozens of career officials who had known about the lead azide for months handled it appropriately.

In public, the administration took a victory lap. "Reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," the White House posted.

Reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations. pic.twitter.com/RofoAsamc3

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 25, 2026

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, who CBS says spent the weekend calling officials, Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand among them, went further: "What President Trump's team achieved in Iowa in the face of an acute public safety hazard - the perfect precision of engineering, chemistry, construction, weather analysis, health science, and the most sophisticated explosives technology - will be studied for generations to come."

What President Trump's team achieved in Iowa in the face of an acute public safety hazard - the perfect precision of engineering, chemistry, construction, weather analysis, health science, and the most sophisticated explosives technology - will be studied for generations to come.

— Stephen Miller (@StephenM) November 25, 2026

Vice President JD Vance gave the credit to Miller, "whose leadership was instrumental in making tough decisions and averting potential disaster."

Credit to our great Chief of Staff Stephen Miller whose leadership was instrumental in making tough decisions and averting potential disaster. Where other administrations failed to act, President Trump's confronted the task at hand. No one passed the buck. This team stepped up... https://t.co/zH1Ymqfow8

— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 25, 2026

The blast went off at 9 a.m. Central. Within 15 minutes the EPA's air monitors showed no airborne lead, and more than an hour later the agency said "ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region."

At 9:00am CT, @USArmy Sustainment Command executed the controlled mitigated detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region. EPA monitors never stopped collecting...

— U.S. EPA (@EPA) November 25, 2026

The detonation "wildly exceeded my expectations," said Major General Eric Shirley, who commands Army Sustainment Command, adding that every barrel of lead azide was destroyed with no secondary explosions or damage to the plant, according to the Associated Press. FEMA's all clear followed that evening.

UPDATE: @FEMA has issued an All Clear around Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. DTRA maps indicate ZERO airborne lead detection following this morning's controlled detonation. 

Post-detonation surface sampling is underway, and results will be released once complete. pic.twitter.com/qgxitd6l28

— U.S. Army (@USArmy) November 25, 2026

Crews had worked around the clock ahead of the blast, the Army said, building a water wall filled with more than 100,000 gallons of water, earth berms and sand-filled blocks around the site.

U.S. Army personnel are on site in Middletown, Iowa, and have worked around the clock to mitigate the impacts of the planned controlled detonation later this morning.

This includes a water wall filled with more than 100,000 gallons of water, earth berms, sand filled blocks,... pic.twitter.com/eQa3erwlXj

— U.S. Army (@USArmy) November 25, 2026

The Army says post-detonation surface sampling is underway and that results "will be released once complete," with no date given, and the EPA, which took more than 1,200 air, land and water samples before the blast, kept sampling on Wednesday afternoon. David Cwiertny, a University of Iowa engineering professor whose team is running its own air and soil monitoring, told CNN: "The biggest question is, what is the timeline at which this all gets returned back?" He said lab work takes anywhere from 24 hours, if expedited, to longer, and the holiday could slow it down.

Dr. Dan McCabe, medical director of the Iowa Poison Control Center, told the network "there needs to be surface testing, soil testing," rolling out over the coming days to weeks, because even small amounts of lead can cause long-term harm to children and pregnant women.

About 350 farms sat under the projected plume, according to the USDA. Doug Seyb, a 71-year-old cattle farmer in Donnellson, told the AP his herd was on pasture and couldn't be brought in. 

"All of these cows are pregnant," he said, worried about birth defects in his calves and lead in his crops.

Governor-elect Rob Sand, the Democrat who takes office in January and who had no authority over the detonation, said the lead-up "should never have been so chaotic and unclear" and called for "immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did." Trump answered that Sand had "hurt and delayed the process," CBS reported. On Monday the president had warned he would hold Sand responsible "for any and all death or destruction" if he stood in the way, before Sand punted the decision back to Washington.

There is obviously more testing to do that will provide certainty over time, but for now, federal officials have reported that lead dispersal should be limited, Iowans are safe, and damage to property is limited. I'm grateful to the experts on the ground who did all they could to...

— Rob Sand (@RobSandIA) November 25, 2026

The Army told the EPA in March that a routine inspection had found 68 barrels of degraded lead azide, crystallized to the point of being more sensitive to friction, shock and cold. Eight months later the Army was urging Middletown to evacuate, as we reported last week, then a federal appeals court froze the EPA's permit, Trump put the blast on hold, and the court let it go ahead, all inside a week.

The Iowa Environmental Council, which sued to stop it, says "Iowa and neighboring states deserve a full accounting." Until the soil numbers are out, no one in Middletown knows whether there is anything left to clean up.

items.title: Houthis Target Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Port Of Jeddah For First Time Ever
items.content_text:
Houthis Target Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Port Of Jeddah For First Time Ever

Via The Cradle

The Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF/Houthis) announced on Wednesday its first operation targeting the Saudi port of Jeddah, in response to the kingdom’s recent airstrikes on Hodeidah Port. 

The YAF also announced a second operation targeting the Saudi port of Jizan, "as part of the response to the Saudi aggression against our country, and in retaliation for its targeting of the port of Hodeidah, and in order to establish the equation of port for port."

Both attacks were “accurate” and “resulted in damage to the targeted sites,” the YAF added. It stressed that it “will not hesitate to respond directly and immediately to any aggression targeting the port of Hodeidah” and “will continue to establish deterrence equations, whatever the consequences and repercussions.”

Both facilities are vital to the kingdom and are situated on Saudi Arabia’s western Red Sea coast. The Saudi-led coalition claimed it intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the Yemeni army near Jeddah Islamic Port, but acknowledged that a projectile struck the port of Jizan. It said the strike caused minor damage.

Unverified videos on social media allegedly showed fires breaking out at the Jeddah facility. This was the first YAF operation ever targeting the Saudi port of Jeddah. 

The kingdom launched a heavy attack on the western Yemeni port of Hodeidah early on 25 November. Attacks also targeted Sanaa International Airport. The Yemeni army (Houthis) had warned earlier that all Saudi ports would become targets if Hodeidah Port came under renewed aggression.

Since the kingdom’s escalation of its decade-long war on Yemen in July, oil refineries, energy storage sites, military bases, and airports across Saudi Arabia have been targeted.

The YAF has heavily targeted Saudi energy infrastructure across the kingdom and has launched multiple attacks on the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, targeting refineries and energy facilities operated by Riyadh.

Sanaa has vowed to continue its operations against sites within Saudi Arabia, as well as its advance on the ground inside Yemen, which recently saw its forces seize Bab al-Mandab from the kingdom’s proxies. 

The Yemeni army (Houthis) now controls the entire western coast of the country, giving it increased leverage over Saudi and Israeli shipping in the Red Sea.

Riyadh is preparing for its war against Yemen to “stretch well into next year,” despite the setbacks it has faced in the conflict, two western officials were cited by Reuters as saying on 18 November. Over 450 people have been killed in Yemen by the Saudi-led coalition since July 2026, according to the Yemeni Health Ministry.

items.title: Father And Son Who Scammed IRS Out Of $46 Million Plead Guilty... And The Son Even Rapped About It
items.content_text:
Father And Son Who Scammed IRS Out Of $46 Million Plead Guilty... And The Son Even Rapped About It

A Long Island father and son have pleaded guilty in what prosecutors call the largest Employee Retention Credit fraud case in the country: more than 8,000 fake employment tax returns that sought over $600 million in pandemic relief credits, of which the IRS paid out about $46 million.

Keith Williams, 48, and his son Jamari Lewis, 28, both of West Hempstead, New York, ran the scheme out of Credit Reset, a purported credit repair business Williams owned, according to the Justice Department. Williams pleaded guilty on Nov. 24 to conspiracy to defraud the United States and wire fraud. Lewis pleaded guilty to wire fraud on Nov. 19 and is set to be sentenced on April 19, 2027.

New York Father and Son Plead GUILTY in $600M Covid Tax Fraud Scheme

"Today's guilty pleas underscore the Fraud Division's commitment to holding accountable those who steal from the American people." -@AAGMcDonald

Read more: https://t.co/zYAwsw6OWy pic.twitter.com/BAxQY6PB1U

— National Fraud Enforcement Division (@DOJFraudDiv) November 24, 2026

"Taxpayer-funded pandemic relief was meant to help businesses and workers in need, not to bankroll fraud schemes," said Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who heads the department's National Fraud Enforcement Division.

The pair worked two programs Congress created during the pandemic: the Employee Retention Credit, meant to keep workers on payroll, and the paid sick and family leave credit. Acting as tax preparers for themselves and their clients, they filed returns that claimed sick and family leave credits larger than the wages reported, counted the same wages as both sick leave and family leave, or claimed both credits on the same wages, according to prosecutors. They were paid in Treasury refund checks and in fees or a cut of each client's refund, and the recruiters they brought in got a percentage of the checks too.

When prosecutors in the Eastern District of New York charged seven people in January 2025, they said the returns, filed from November 2021 to June 2023, were mostly for shell businesses with no real operations or employees. Prosecutors said the money went on jewelry, electronics, designer clothing and luxury cars.

Lewis, an aspiring rapper who performs as "Mr. Chaketah," posted a song called "I'm Really Sophisticated (IRS)," with the IRS logo on its album cover, according to the indictment announcement. In a recorded call with a co-conspirator, Williams compared the scheme to "taking candy from a baby," prosecutors said.

Agents who searched Williams' home seized designer goods from Rolex, Gucci, Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Balenciaga and Versace, along with a Land Rover, a Polaris Slingshot and a Tesla Model Y, all of which prosecutors said appeared to have been bought with the proceeds.

As part of their plea deals, both men agreed to pay the IRS $46,756,084.89 in restitution. Williams also agreed to forfeit $4,848,998.44 and Lewis $671,511.11. Williams faces up to five years on the conspiracy count and up to 30 years on wire fraud; Lewis faces up to 30 years.

Co-defendant Janine Davis pleaded guilty to wire fraud in May, and Tiffany Williams, a 43-year-old Brooklyn tax preparer, was sentenced to 36 months in prison the same month.

items.title: "This Is A Cyber Attack. All Day": Hackers Call BS On Official Story After NSA, FAA, Microsoft And Banks Go Dark
items.content_text:
"This Is A Cyber Attack. All Day": Hackers Call BS On Official Story After NSA, FAA, Microsoft And Banks Go Dark

Authored by Russ Jones via The Epoch Times,

In a span of 10 days, Microsoft's email went dark for millions, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded every departing flight in the country, and customers at U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Chase, and Bank of America could not move money. The National Security Agency's internal communications network went down, and Delta Air Lines delayed flights nationwide due to problems with its weigh-and-balance automation system. Meanwhile, the FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its database, which police across the country use to check criminal records.

To many Americans, the events of Nov. 12 to Nov. 22 looked like a pattern. To the government, it is a run of bad luck.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Nov. 18 that the incidents "are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is "zero" evidence the outages are linked or caused by hackers.

Some veteran cybersecurity experts aren't buying it.

Rodney Gullatte Jr., a certified ethical hacker, Air Force veteran, and CEO of Firma IT Solutions, said the moment the NSA network failed, he stopped hedging.

"I'm no longer being quiet about the fact that this is definitely a cyber attack happening right now," Gullatte told The Epoch Times.

Companies hire Gullatte to break into their systems so they can find the holes before criminals do. He said the professional hackers he talks with reached the same conclusion early, when the FAA went down. Their verdict, he said, was simple: "This is a cyber attack. All day."

Stuart Madnick, a professor of information technology at MIT's Sloan School of Management and founding director of the Cybersecurity at MIT Sloan research consortium, is more cautious but shares the suspicion.

"It is possible that this was all just a lot of coincidences," Madnick told The Epoch Times. "But these are particularly peculiar coincidences."

Others who have spent careers inside the world of hacking see something far more ordinary at work: routine software updates gone wrong.

A Week of Failures

The trouble began on Nov. 12, when Microsoft 365 went down worldwide. Outlook was knocked offline for close to 24 hours, while Teams, Copilot, and other services were affected to a lesser degree. In a post-incident report, Microsoft blamed a software defect in its networking gateway servers that had sat unnoticed since July, combined with a shift in network traffic and an issue that reduced capacity.

The next day, the FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours after a telecommunications failure. Three days later, Chase said a software bug disrupted its services. Later that week, the NSA said it experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" that affected some internal systems.

Every organization involved has said its outage was not a cyberattack.

Still, the pileup has rattled the public. Vice President JD Vance said friends have asked him whether they should build a bunker or stock up on food and water.

"My answer is no. We don't see a crisis coming down," Vance said on Nov. 16. "But you have to be prepared for everything."

President Donald Trump brushed off the concerns.

"When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen," he told reporters on Nov. 17 in Manila. "It's fine."

Q: Are you concerned about all these outages - Microsoft, United, Chase Bank?

TRUMP: "It's life. When you're big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen - it's fine." pic.twitter.com/NQNAgJ58dE

— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 17, 2026

'Peculiar Coincidences'

Madnick stressed that he has no inside information. But he said the cluster of failures is hard to dismiss.

"I can never rule out the possibility of this being just an incredible set of circumstances," he said. "But if I'm a betting man, I would say this is a highly unlikely sequence of events."

The FAA has issued nationwide shutdowns only a handful of times in the past two decades, he said, and banks have had problems before.

What stands out is the timing.

"Never so many in such a short period of time," Madnick said.

He also questioned the speed with which officials ruled out foul play. When events like these happen, he said, the first announcement usually says it definitely was not a cyberattack. The second says no one yet knows what happened.

"Which makes me wonder how they could say announcement number one," he said.

For Gullatte, the Microsoft outage alone was not surprising. Russian state hackers have targeted the company before. More recently, he said, criminals stole a key that connected a third-party email backup service to Microsoft 365 and used it to get into about 2,200 business accounts. The key was changed, he said, but no one knows what the intruders did once inside, and the story went quiet.

"Then the next thing we hear is the global outage of Microsoft," he said.

Then came the FAA and bank outages. When a local TV station asked Gullatte to call it a cyberattack after Chase went down, he declined. The NSA outage changed his mind. Asked why he doesn't accept the official explanations, Gullatte said his job won't let him.

"My profession is threat intel, and there are companies and people that depend on me to see threats before they're upon us," he said. "I can't afford not to look at this as anything other than a coordinated attack."

He also believes officials would not say so even if it were. "They don't want to cause a panic with the public," he said. "If you don't have the clearance, you're not going to find out."

Capability, Opportunity, and Motive

Madnick, whose research on computer security dates to 1979, said a major cyberattack needs three things: capability, opportunity, and motive.

For years, plenty of adversaries had the first two, he said. What they lacked was a reason to act. Rising global tensions may be changing that.

He compared the risk to the 2024 attack in Lebanon, when Israel set off thousands of pagers and hundreds of walkie-talkies in back-to-back attacks on Sept. 17 and 18 that year. Those devices had been rigged in advance, he said, and the trigger was pulled when the moment was right.

The FBI has warned that foreign groups are probing U.S. systems, Madnick said.

"But maybe it wasn't just probing," he said. "Maybe it was planting time bombs or land mines and just waiting for the time that's right to pull the plug."

He was careful to qualify that statement as supposition.

"I've got no hard evidence," he said, "but the circumstance is definitely consistent with that."

Artificial intelligence raises the stakes. Gullatte said anyone can now buy a ransomware kit on the dark web for a few hundred dollars, along with lists of vulnerable companies and even a criminal "help desk." AI removes the last barrier.

"You can bring up AI and be like, I want you to go hack into that website," he said. "Press enter. No technical nothing. And this thing will create a swarm of AI agents and just attack it."

'Never Ascribe to Malice'

Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker who is now vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy and a faculty member at IANS Research, sees the same AI trend producing a very different result.

AI is uncovering more security flaws, he said, so companies are installing fixes on more complicated systems. Every update carries a small chance of breaking something.

"If there's a base rate, and we do more of it, we're going to have more outages," Williams told The Epoch Times.

He said he fully believes Microsoft's account. Software that runs thousands of tasks at once can pass every test and still crash under real-world traffic.

"I've experienced that exact thing myself," he said.

When companies hire him to determine whether a failure was an attack, his first question is where the evidence is. The starting point must be some sign that an outsider got in without permission.

A nation-state could, in theory, disguise an attack as a routine bug, he said, but doing it without leaving a digital trail is "really, really difficult."

He believes people are now noticing outages they have usually missed in the past. Amtrak's apps and websites, he said, go down often.

"Never ascribe to malice what can be ascribed to incompetence," Williams said. "If there was an indication this was a cyberattack, they would be screaming it from the rooftops."

Gullatte doesn't dismiss that view. Many organizations still run outdated systems, he said, and a major upgrade pushed straight into service without a test run can bring a whole system down.

Asked whether the country is in a cyberwar, both men gave nearly the same answer from opposite directions.

"If we're in a cyber war now, we're in a cyber war always," Williams said.

"We've been in the cyber war for a long time," Gullatte said. "People only really care about it when the media talks about it."

A Problem Either Way

All three experts agree the country is too fragile, accident or not.

"A thousand percent," Williams said when asked whether the Microsoft outage is a national security issue.

He said he is surprised Congress has not called Microsoft executives to testify. Many federal agencies, he noted, run on separate government versions of Microsoft's cloud that, to his knowledge, stayed up.

"If a simple accident could cause so much disruption, something isn't quite right," Madnick said. "Imagine [if] someone wanted to do it deliberately."

He pointed to the 2024 cyberattack on Change Healthcare, a little-known company that connects pharmacies to insurers. When it went down, patients across the country could not get prescriptions approved.

"We are heavily interconnected and interdependent, often in ways we're not aware of," he said.

Plan B

Madnick said the answer is preparation, not panic. Companies need tested backups and a quick way to undo a failed upgrade. Families should assume disruptions will happen.

"If there's a snowstorm coming and you don't have a snow shovel in your garage, you'd be silly," said Madnick, who lives in the Northeast. "We need to realize these things can happen and say, 'What is our plan B?'"

Gullatte skipped a happy-hour the day the FAA went down and bought cases of water at Costco instead. If pulling some cash from an ATM or stocking water calms people down, he said, they should do it.

His bigger advice is digital. Use a different, long password for every account, turn on two-factor authentication with an authenticator app, set up passkeys and freeze your credit. Because AI can now clone a voice, he said, give the credit bureaus a secret word to unlock it.

Neither expert who suspects an attack expects the outages to stop.

"There's more to come," Gullatte said. Madnick said he hopes the recent outages mark the end of it. But he has been warning for more than a decade that the trend runs the other way.

"The worst is yet to come," Madnick said, "because each year, the situation is worse than the previous year."

items.title: Americans Set To Put A Record $21 Billion Of Christmas On Buy-Now-Pay-Later... Mostly From Their Phones
items.content_text:
Americans Set To Put A Record $21 Billion Of Christmas On Buy-Now-Pay-Later... Mostly From Their Phones

Adobe expects American shoppers to put a record $21.3 billion of their online holiday spending on buy now, pay later loans this season, up 6.6% from last year, according to its forecast for Nov. 1 through Dec. 31.

On Cyber Monday alone, shoppers are expected to finance $1.09 billion online, the second year in a row BNPL tops $1 billion on Cyber Monday. Black Friday adds another $807 million. And 82% of BNPL spending will come through phones rather than desktops, which Adobe chalks up to "impulse shopping."

BNPL drove $20 billion of online holiday spending last season, up nearly 10%, as we reported in January, and Cyber Monday 2025 was the biggest BNPL day on record, at over $1 billion.

The loans ride on a bigger number: Adobe sees Americans spending $275.1 billion online this holiday season, up 6.7%, with Cyber Week, the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, bringing in $47.5 billion (up 7.4%), or 17.3% of the season.

Thanksgiving Day itself is set to drive $6.9 billion online, up 8.5%, and a record 63% of it is expected to come through mobile devices, up from 61.6% last year, against 57.4% for the season as a whole. Black Friday is forecast at $12.9 billion (up 9.2%), growing faster than Cyber Monday, which should still be the biggest day of the season at $15.1 billion (up 6.2%).

Adobe puts that Black Friday growth down in part to the biggest discounts of the season on TVs, apparel and appliances. Discounts overall are expected to top out at 30% off listed price during Cyber Week, on par with 2025. Electronics and computers get their deepest cuts on Cyber Monday; TVs, toys, apparel, appliances and furniture on Black Friday; and sporting goods on Thanksgiving.

A good chunk of the haul won't be gifts: during Cyber Week, online sales of personal hygiene products are expected to jump 150% over their average September levels, with clothing basics up 210%, baby products 113%, pet products 93% and household cleaning items 49%, as shoppers use the deals to stock up on essentials.

We've seen where that leads: a quarter of BNPL users had used the loans to buy groceries in a LendingTree survey last year, up from 14% a year earlier, and 41% said they had paid late in the past year, up from 34%, as we noted at the time.

Adobe also expects traffic to US retail sites from AI tools (shoppers clicking a link) to rise 130% this season, led by Thanksgiving (up 159%), Black Friday (up 95%) and Cyber Monday (up 88%). In an Adobe survey of 5,000 consumers, 77% of those who had used AI to shop said they felt more confident in their purchase.

The forecast is Adobe's from Sept. 28; the real numbers start landing over the long weekend. Last season came in at a record $257.8 billion online, beating Adobe's own forecast by $4.4 billion.

items.title: Venezuela Admits Its $237.5 Billion Debt Is Unsustainable
items.content_text:
Venezuela Admits Its $237.5 Billion Debt Is Unsustainable

Authored by Evgenia Filimianova via The Epoch Times,

Venezuela has set out a plan to restructure $237.5 billion in debt, restore stability, and more than double its oil output.

Caracas said in a macroeconomic framework published on Tuesday that the country's total debt, about 242 percent of GDP, is unsustainable and that Venezuela has been in protracted default since 2017.

Venezuela's economy has been battered by years of hyperinflation, sanctions and, most recently, deadly earthquakes.

Venezuela, currently led by interim leader Delcy Rodríguez since the U.S. military captured former leader Nicolás Maduro in January, said it would pursue a single, comprehensive restructuring of debt owed by both the state and state oil company PDVSA, but did not specify how much relief it is seeking.

The largest block is about $110 billion in Eurobonds, around $46 billion of it unpaid interest. The rest comprises arbitration claims, bilateral and multilateral loans, bank debt, and PDVSA's supplier, pension, and other nonfinancial liabilities, some of which are owed within the public sector.

Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude reserves, more than 300 billion barrels, but produced only about 1 million barrels a day in 2025, down from around 3.5 million in the 1990s.

The plan projects output reaching 2.9 million barrels a day by 2036, with GDP growth averaging 6.3 percent a year over the decade. It also expects the economy to grow 5 percent this year.

An oil agreement between the United States and Venezuela, announced in August, is a key component of that forecast.

It covers 17 oilfields holding roughly 65 billion barrels. North American Blue Energy Partners would fund their development, and the U.S. government would take a 35 percent stake in its parent company. The deal could generate more than $200 billion in revenue for the Venezuelan state over 25 years, according to the framework.

Earlier this month, ExxonMobil signed a memorandum of understanding with PDVSA to assess upstream opportunities, a potential return to a country that expropriated its assets almost two decades ago.

The agreement is nonbinding and commits the U.S. company to no specific project, and Exxon has not said which areas it is examining. It would need a final joint-venture or production-sharing contract before taking part in exploration or production.

Exxon described the memorandum as a meaningful first step, but said any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections, and competitive returns.

Venezuela has also amended its hydrocarbons law, lowering the maximum combined royalty and tax rate and adding alternative dispute-resolution mechanisms for investors.

Phased Reforms

The plan is organized into three phases: 12 months of normalization, two years of recovery, and longer-term diversification.

Early priorities include unifying the exchange rate, publishing central bank accounts, introducing fiscal rules, and overhauling tax collection. Another early goal is a push to attract Venezuelans living abroad back home.

Later goals include a sovereign wealth fund to manage oil income.

The government said it expects to eliminate the public-sector primary deficit by 2031 and to double the dollar value of the economy to about $200 billion by then.

It acknowledged that inflation, which stood at 475 percent at the end of last year, is expected to accelerate this year before converging to about 24 percent over the medium term.

The government's own risk assessment lists slow oil recovery, oil price swings, delayed debt talks, weak administrative capacity, and the persistence of sanctions among the threats, though it describes overall risks as moderate.

Earthquake Aftermath

Earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 in magnitude hit the country on June 24, killing more than 6,000 people and leaving about 18,000 homeless.

The World Bank has put direct physical damage at about $19.6 billion and, according to Caracas, about $10 billion of reconstruction costs will fall on the public sector, spread over roughly five years.

Oil and gas infrastructure was not materially damaged, the document said.

Washington has pledged more than $386 million in humanitarian aid, and the International Monetary Fund facilitated access to about $346 million of Venezuela's reserve tranche.

items.title: Zelensky Says He Will Seek More Military Aid From New Dem-Controlled Congress

Zelensky Says He Will Seek More Military Aid From New Dem-Controlled Congress

Authored by Dave DeCamp via AntiWar.com

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has told Bloomberg that he will seek a robust military aid package from the US Congress when Democrats take control of both the House and the Senate this January if no peace deal is reached with Russia.

Zelensky’s comments come a few weeks after the Financial Times reported that Democrats were considering a $15 billion military aid package for Ukraine and suggested it could be pushed during the lame-duck period, before the new Congress is sworn in.

Zelensky will also seek tougher sanctions on Russia, and a congressional aide told the FT that Democrats will seek to amend the Russia sanctions and tariff bill named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, as President Trump has chosen not to implement the sanctions and tariffs under a mechanism included in the legislation.

"We’re going to fix the Graham bill," a Democratic aide on the House Foreign Affairs Committee told FT. "A year and a half was spent trying to get sanctions on Russia, and they were waived away."

Zelensky told Bloomberg that Ukraine has been urging its supporters to provide more interceptors for at least December, as he expects more support from the US come the New Year. 

"Please cover our needs for at least the whole of December," he said. "Why? Because I'm still counting on being able to find, so to speak, a new approach to the new Congress in January or February."

As things stand, a peace deal to end the war appears unlikely as Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and the lead US negotiator, continues to insist that Russia is open to the West providing Ukraine with NATO Article 5-style security guarantees despite Russia’s rejection of the idea.

For his part, Zelensky continues to insist that Ukraine should be fully admitted into NATO and has shown no willingness to make concessions. The Ukrainian leader is signaling that he will leverage the incoming Congress to push back against concessions that the Trump administration may want him to make.

Capitol Hill Erupts Over American Billionaire's Govt-Backed Buyout Of Lukoil's Global Assets Using Frozen Russian Securities

Congressional Democrats are outraged over after a group of investors led by American pro-Trump billionaire Todd Boehly has signed an agreement to acquire the sanctioned international assets of Russian oil giant Lukoil.

The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks, is demanding answers of the Trump administration over the participation of the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) in the proposed acquisition. Meeks blasted the transaction as a "shameful deal".

"Congress banned the DFC from investing in Russia less than a year ago, yet this Administration is circumventing that restriction by buying $10 billion in energy assets from Russia’s largest oil company [note: it's actually the second-largest], a corporation the US sanctioned precisely to pressure Moscow to end its war in Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement. 

As a reminder, the DFC is basically the international investment arm of the US government, utilizing private capital to support economic development that serves 'US interests'.

For some further details of the deal, it is valued at approximately $16 billion, and centers on the purchase of Austria-registered Lukoil International GmbH, which is the holding entity through which Moscow’s second-largest oil producer controls the bulk of its global footprint. 

The deal comes after more than a year of negotiations, and still faces the major regulatory hurdle of a final sign-off from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The buying group combines private capital with direct US government backing, including the following: Eldridge - which is Boehly’s private investment firm, Xtellus Partners - an American investment bank, Catena Investment Holding - an investment firm based in the UAE, and most cointroversially the aforementioned US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC).

Instead of paying in cash, Reuters has described the buyers devised a workaround to get around Western sanctions. The group bought roughly $10 billion in frozen Russian stocks and bonds - assets locked up since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine - from US and British financial firms. They plan to trade those trapped securities for Lukoil's assets and place them into a special account in the UAE.

Critics accuse the Trump family of using Ukraine negotiations, spearheaded by the Kushner-Witkoff team, ultimately as cover to scoop up massive spoils...

While as mentioned the assets are estimated to be worth $16 billion, the final price will shift depending on global oil prices. Boehly has indicated that finalizing the deal could take up to a year, and the company will be renamed once the sale is complete.

items.title: Thank You, Capitalism
items.content_text:
Thank You, Capitalism

Authored by John Stossel via The Epoch Times,

Happy Thanksgiving!

The cost of the average Thanksgiving dinner went up 6 percent this year.

Blame politicians who create inflation by printing more money.

But then, thank capitalists, who keep finding ways to deliver food for less.

Walmart offers a complete Thanksgiving meal for 10 for $35. Aldi sells one for $39.

A better way to compare costs is to look at how long you have to work to buy something.

In 1986, a blue-collar worker had to work 3.22 hours to buy a Thanksgiving meal. Today, just 1.79 hours.

Most of life improves.

I'm thankful for that.

And thankful that, in the United States today, charity and food are so plentiful that no one needs to go hungry.

It wasn't always this way. For most of history, hunger was the norm. That was true here, too.

When the Pilgrims landed in Plymouth, they planned a harmonious new society where everyone shared everything. Socialism!

Their first year in America, they pooled and shared the harvest equally, regardless of how much anyone worked.

The results were disastrous.

Few Pilgrims worked hard. People relied on someone else to do the heavy lifting.

Gov. William Bradford wrote that some pilgrims faked illness, claiming "weakness and inability," and "much was stolen."

The communal system, Bradford concluded, "was found to breed much confusion and discontent and retard much employment." Nearly half the colony died that first winter.

Had the Wampanoag Native Americans not helped them, more would have starved.

Economists call this the "Tragedy of the Commons."

Imagine ranchers sharing a common pasture. Each has an incentive to add more cattle to maximize his own herd. Soon, the extra animals eat all the grass, the pasture is ruined, and everyone loses.

Yet many Americans vote for the very system that almost starved the Pilgrims.

Forty-three percent now view socialism positively, the highest rating since Gallup began tracking it. Among young adults, 57 percent prefer socialism to capitalism.

Americans should know we already tried socialism. The only reason we get to celebrate Thanksgiving with an abundance of food is because the Pilgrims learned the hard way that socialism doesn't work.

Sharing "public" property sounds good, but only private ownership incentivizes people to work and conserve.

Desperate to save the colony, Bradford abandoned the Pilgrims' socialist experiment. "Every family," he wrote, "was assigned a parcel of land" to grow their own crops.

Private property! Capitalism!

Before you eat that turkey on Thursday, thank private property! 

Without it, Thanksgiving would be: "Starvation Day."

Here's why: pic.twitter.com/s9SWmUNydh

— John Stossel (@JohnStossel) November 24, 2026

Miraculously, the people who claimed "weakness and inability" recovered.

Bradford wrote about the transformation: "It made all hands very industrious, so as much more corn was planted than otherwise would have been .... The women now went willingly into the field, and took their little ones with them to set corn."

Of course they did. Now they got to keep what they produced.

Shortages turned into surplus. That surplus became the abundance we celebrate now.

But now it's something most of us take for granted.

Americans today spend less than 10 percent of their disposable income on food. A century ago, families spent nearly a quarter of their income just to eat.

This abundance didn't happen because smart people in Washington managed the food supply or set "fair" prices. Government can barely manage a DMV line.

It happens because of capitalism: Millions of free people make billions of voluntary exchanges. Farmers innovate to grow more crops on less land. Truckers, warehouse workers and grocers move food across the country with incredible precision. Airlines compete to drive down fares so you can fly home to see your family.

Greedy entrepreneurs get rich by figuring out how to make things cheaper, faster and better for the rest of us.

On Thanksgiving, when you sit down to eat, take a moment to appreciate what's actually on your plate - the miracle of free markets.

items.title: Biden Judge Freezes Carr's War On ABC: 'This Is Not A Close Case'
items.content_text:
Biden Judge Freezes Carr's War On ABC: 'This Is Not A Close Case'

A federal judge in Washington on Wednesday blocked the FCC from pressing ahead with its early review of the broadcast licenses of ABC's eight owned stations, finding Disney is likely to prove the review was retaliation for coverage President Trump didn't like.

"This is not a close case," U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan wrote in a 45-page opinion that also threw out the FCC's motion to dismiss Disney's lawsuit. Her order bars the commission from "any continuing or further action" against the stations in the early renewal proceedings, "including issuing a Hearing Designation Order" - the step that would have sent the licenses to an evidentiary hearing.

AliKhan saved her sharpest words for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. "Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," she wrote, noting that the same week Trump tapped him to run the agency, after months of Trump calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" over its campaign coverage, Carr praised "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct."

The FCC's Media Bureau ordered the stations on April 28 to file their renewals years ahead of schedule; the licenses weren't due until 2028 at the earliest. That came the day after Trump attacked a Jimmy Kimmel skit about the First Lady. "It is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings," AliKhan wrote, citing "President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response."

She quoted Carr's own words back to him. After the order went out, he said: "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should." After Kimmel's September 2025 remarks about Trump and his supporters, he said: "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead."

Carr has said the early review grew out of the agency's probe of Disney's diversity, equity and inclusion practices. AliKhan found the agency reached for the "harshest" tool available, one it "had not used in over half a century," which she said bolstered her "finding of pretext." The FCC's own supplemental brief admitted there were other ways to order an evidentiary hearing.

The judge also rejected the FCC's argument that a company with Disney's money couldn't be chilled. "Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness - wealthy or not - would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business," she wrote.

In July, when the White House asked networks to carry Trump's primetime address on "election interference," ABC streamed it online instead of airing it, and Carr said the FCC was "looking into" that decision as part of the renewal proceedings. Since the Media Bureau opened its February probe of The View, "no candidate for public office has appeared" on the show, according to a Disney declaration the judge cited, and ABC now weighs every political booking for whether the FCC "might later" cite it against the licenses.

AliKhan did decline to bar the FCC from "any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten" ABC beyond the renewal proceedings, saying Disney hadn't spelled out what those might be. She set a $1 bond and gave the FCC until Dec. 2 to report on how it is complying.

The FCC said the ruling "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," a spokesperson told NBC News. "We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added. ABC called it "an important victory for the First Amendment."

Anna Gomez, the FCC's lone Democrat, said the decision "shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights."

NEWS: A federal court has stopped the FCC from continuing it's censorship campaign against ABC.

This brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Rf1SdMdxhJ

— Anna M. Gomez (@AGomezFCC) November 26, 2026

Disney sued in August, arguing the FCC used the early reviews to apply "maximal coercive pressure" on ABC while dodging the courts. Carr has defended the review and told NBC News the suit was a "meritless case." The FCC is separately still reviewing whether The View broke the equal-time rule for political candidates, which the injunction doesn't touch.

items.title: Over $280 Million Worth Of Marijuana Seized In California Raid
items.content_text:
Over $280 Million Worth Of Marijuana Seized In California Raid

Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times,

A Bureau of Land Management (BLM)-led probe in California has led to the confiscation of more than 117 tons of processed marijuana with an estimated street value of around $282.8 million.

Investigators seized the drugs on Nov. 17 after serving a search warrant at multiple industrial warehouses in Chico, California. They discovered equipment used to de-stem, sort, and process marijuana flowers in the warehouses, with the processed marijuana found stored in boxes, large crates, and other containers. A total of 62 individuals were arrested for cultivation of marijuana in the crackdown, the Department of the Interior (DOI) said in a Nov. 24 statement.

Investigators alleged the warehouses were part of a larger network engaged in growing, processing, and distributing marijuana across California's northern region, including on lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service and the BLM.

The seizure underscores the extent of this network's alleged marijuana cultivation and distribution operations in northern California, the department said.

The operation advances the Trump administration's aim to eliminate illegal drug activities and restore safety in public lands, DOI said.

"America's public lands are set aside for the benefit and enjoyment of the American people, and it's our duty to keep them safe," Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in the statement.

"Interior will not tolerate criminals exploiting federal property. We're grateful for the dedication of our brave Bureau of Land Management agents and our local, state and federal partners for shutting down this illegal enterprise," Burgum said.

An earlier law enforcement crackdown in northern California disrupted a major narcotics operation in the state, leading to the confiscation of significant quantities of cocaine and fentanyl, the DOI said in a July 13 statement. The crackdown was part of efforts to counter drug trafficking in public lands managed by the BLM.

The fentanyl seized during the operation represented over 1.2 million potentially fatal doses.

Rep. James Gallagher (R-Calif.) called on FBI director Kash Patel last month to investigate transnational criminal groups running thousands of marijuana sites in California's Siskiyou and Shasta counties, highlighting that illegal cultivation has been documented on federal land, according to an Oct. 19 statement from the lawmaker's office.

Almost one million illegally cultivated cannabis plants were eradicated in California this year and 221 arrests have been made across 22 counties in the state under the Eradication and Prevention of Illicit Cannabis (EPIC) program, state Attorney General Rob Bonta's office said in a Nov. 16 statement.

"EPIC is the only task force in California that brings local, state and federal partners together to combat illegal cannabis cultivation on public lands," Thomas French, Bureau of Land Management Special Agent in Charge for Region 1-California, said in the statement, which described EPIC's work as disrupting the activities of organized criminal groups and rescuing individuals who were forced into labor.

"An illegal grow can divert a stream and leave toxic chemicals behind long after the plants are gone," French said. "We do this critical work every year so our kids and grandkids can explore these incredible lands and enjoy them the way we do today."

items.title: Watch: Ex-NBA Star Enes Kanter Gets Death Threats Every Couple Hours, Has To Tell FBI Wherever He Goes
items.content_text:
Watch: Ex-NBA Star Enes Kanter Gets Death Threats Every Couple Hours, Has To Tell FBI Wherever He Goes

Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom, three months into his bid to enter the WNBA draft, says the death threats now come "once every couple hours" and that he has to tell the FBI wherever he goes.

"I thought after this whole, you know, China thing, obviously, I was getting death threats every week," Kanter Freedom told Triggernometry hosts Konstantin Kisin and Francis Foster in an episode released Tuesday. "And now I get that threats once every couple hours, you know, these are very, very ugly death threats."

"Now everywhere we have to go, we have to let FBI know where we're going," he said. "My DMs are full of images and videos of the moment that Charlie Kirk got shot. And they're saying that you're going to be next."

Kanter Freedom, who says he was forced out of the NBA over his criticism of China, was answering a question from the hosts: why keep putting himself in that position? "When people say I do what I do for attention, it's disgusting to me because I'm not that crazy," he said. "I'm not going to put my life on risk, you know, to just to get attention from people."

"Think Again"

Later in the hour, he said the threats had already cost him more than his career. An insurer turned down his application for full life coverage a couple of years ago, he said, after he applied because of the death threats he was getting.

"The company came back and said, well, after our research, you have a very high percent chance of getting killed, so we cannot give you the full coverage. We can only give you the health coverage," Kanter Freedom said. "So all these people out there who thinks I do what I do for attention, think again."

He said he has not seen his family in almost 14 years. "Me losing my career, me getting all this, you know, death threats is nothing, nothing compared to not being able to see your mom or your dad or your siblings," he said.

"I'm Going To Make Sure That She Steps Down"

The threats he describes now follow his Aug. 7 declaration for the 2027 WNBA draft, built on the league's collective bargaining agreement, which says only women are eligible and never defines the word. He claimed two other former NBA players, three European players and three G League players "have all said that if they don't change the rules ... then we are all going to put our name in the WNBA draft." Former NBA player Royce White has already declared.

The draw for them, he said, is money: a G League player makes about $45,000 a year, against about $1.6 million for a top WNBA player's contract. His offer to the league: "One, change the rule and I'll walk away and you will not hear from me ever again. Two, draft me and that's it."

Kanter Freedom also took credit for the exit of WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert - but won't say what he did. 

When the league said he couldn't play "because he's a man," he said, "I turned around to my manager. I was like, I'm going to do something and then I'm going to make sure that she steps down in two weeks. She announced her retirement in less than a week. I did what I had to do. I'm not going to tell you what I did."

The NBA announced on Sept. 4 that Engelbert would retire at the end of the year, with Engelbert saying in the release, "I have made the decision to retire." In October she told House Republicans in a letter that "only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men."

The Chicago Sky Suit

Kanter Freedom said his legal fight is with the Chicago Sky, not the league. "I'm a good guy and I do not want to sue the league because the reason is they're already losing millions of dollars every year," he said. "I don't want to bring in a lawsuit and actually bankrupt them."

Security removed him from the Sky's Aug. 23 home game against the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena after a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud, and the team banned him from future games. His federal suit, filed Sept. 3, says he was thrown out over his shirt, which read "WOMAN noun. adult human female," and names the Sky's operating company, the Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority and the City of Chicago.

"What I have done that game, just simply got up and opened my hands and say, I'm here to support them. And then, boom, they kicked me out of the game," Kanter Freedom said. Sky owner Michael Alter has called the suit "meritless and frivolous," saying "Freedom was removed for his conduct, not his speech."

"Over 80, 85 Percent"

"I'm not anti-trans, I'm just pro-woman," Kanter Freedom said, before turning on the league he played in for 11 years. The players' public support for trans athletes is "all a lie," he said, and "over 80, 85 percent of the players are transphobic and homophobic."

"I asked many of them, I was like, would you ever accept a gay player in our team? They said absolutely not," he said. Asked why they never say so, one told him, "if I ever said anything against those people, you know, I'll be canceled," with his endorsement deals "dropped the next day."

He said the same calculation cost him a friend. Colin Kaepernick, he said, "used to send me gifts once a month" and "helped me a lot with how I should fight against the Turkish government." "The day I started to criticize Nike for their hypocrisy and sweatshops and stuff, I never heard from him ever again."

The WNBA draft is in April 2027. Kanter Freedom says he is training every day, and that if a team takes him he will go after Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point record, which he thinks he can break "in one half of the game."

US Renews Travel Alert For Middle East, Says Hostilities Could Rapidly Escalate

Authored by Jack Phillips via The Epoch Times,

The U.S. Department of State on Tuesday renewed an advisory that Americans traveling in the Middle East should be more vigilant due to the increased threat posed by Iran and the Houthis as hostilities in the region continue to simmer.

There is an "increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region," said the State Department in a post through its TravelGov account on X.

Middle East: Americans in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance due to the increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region. Be aware of potential alerts, flight... pic.twitter.com/1ABEg3iGV7

— TravelGov (@TravelGov) November 24, 2026

"Be aware of potential alerts, flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," the department said, adding that Iranian forces recently launched attacks in Kuwait and Bahrain.

Meanwhile, the Iranian-backed, Yemen-based Houthi terrorist group has attacked Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and other infrastructure, the department said.

It further warned that hostilities in the region could rapidly escalate. The department did not provide any specific details about potential attacks.

Col. Majed al-Nuzaily, a spokesman for the Yemeni army, said the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government that withdrew from the western coast of Yemen are now stationed north and west of Aden "on a defense line built to stop the Houthi advance," as the rebels advance within 40 miles of the city.

"Aden is a red line. It was a red line in 2015, when the Houthis came to the city and its people drove them out," he said during a virtual briefing.

Speaking in the same briefing, Yemeni foreign ministry official Marwan al-Noman said the group is a terrorist organization, because the Houthis "threaten Yemenis first and then every nation whose ships cross the Red Sea."

The United States and Israel launched their initial round of strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, leading to a months-long conflict that caused oil and energy prices to surge earlier this year. Iran has attacked or threatened commercial ships in the nearby Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that allows for transportation of roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade.

After the U.S. midterm elections, which saw significant Republican Party losses, U.S. President Donald Trump has signaled that the conflict may end soon. However, he said last week that he believes Tehran will not be willing to make a deal that is acceptable to his administration.

"We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal," he said during a White House news conference on Nov. 20, while he again added that Iran cannot be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.

Trump wrote two days later, on Nov. 22, in a Truth Social post that Iran is becoming more emboldened to launch attacks after the Nov. 3 midterm results. He also questioned why oil prices dropped following the election, claiming "the whole thing is a giant hoax."

Earlier this year, the State Department issued a "worldwide caution" alert for Americans traveling abroad due to escalating tensions in the Middle East. In its last update, issued in July, the agency said U.S. citizens should "exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions" while in the region.

items.title: Refugees, Other Immigrants Sue To Block Trump's Medicaid Cutoff

Refugees, Other Immigrants Sue To Block Trump's Medicaid Cutoff

Authored by Guy Birchall via The Epoch Times,

A group of refugees and other immigrants filed a lawsuit on Tuesday arguing the government cut off their Medicaid coverage through an unlawful interpretation of the president's One Big Beautiful Bill Act from last year.

The proposed nationwide class action suit, filed in a Rhode Island federal court, targets one of the latest efforts by the administration to tighten requirements for government benefits as part of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

The lawsuit challenges guidance from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), part of the HHS, that imposed new eligibility restrictions for Medicaid, barring some lawfully present immigrants.

Illegal immigrants are already ineligible, with an exception for emergency care.

CMS began instructing states in April to terminate Medicaid funding for all legal asylum recipients, refugees, and parolees as of Oct. 1.

According to the lawsuit, Congress left intact eligibility rules for Supplemental Security Income (SSI), which helps low-income elderly or disabled people pay for food and housing, and did not eliminate a requirement that Medicaid benefits be provided to all SSI recipients regardless of immigration status.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs say that as a result, they and other lawfully present immigrants who receive SSI should receive Medicaid coverage.

Amy Romero, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the Lawyers' Committee for Rhode Island, said in a statement that her clients are now "rationing blood pressure pills, skipping heart monitoring, and putting off surgeries because the government unlawfully cut off their health care."

"The government is stripping lifesaving health coverage from some of the most vulnerable people in the country - elderly or disabled refugees, asylees, domestic violence and trafficking victims - without any authority from Congress," she said.

Romero and other attorneys for the plaintiffs argue CMS's interpretation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act is in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act.

They say that one Seattle judge has already ruled that way and issued an injunction blocking cuts for about 800 immigrants on SSI in Washington state. Washington's Health Care Authority projected about 11,000 lawfully present immigrants would lose coverage as of Oct. 1.

The Rhode Island lawsuit seeks the same relief on a nationwide basis by Dec. 22, ahead of a year-end deadline for states to submit their Medicaid plans to HHS.

The plaintiffs seek class certification, arguing that there are so many people affected nationwide that it would be impractical to list plaintiffs individually; the people in the group share the same main legal question; the five named plaintiffs have the same kind of claim as everyone else in the group; and those five plaintiffs can fairly represent the whole group.

The named plaintiffs are from Sudan, the Republic of Congo, Uzbekistan, Turkey, and Ukraine.

The Lawyers' Committee for Rhode Island was joined by the National Health Law Program and the ACLU of Rhode Island.

The Epoch Times contacted HHS for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

Mark Rutte is a completely ridiculous character 👇

items.title: 'Not One Single Person On This Planet Can Be Trusted With Power': AI Is COVID 2.0
items.content_text:
'Not One Single Person On This Planet Can Be Trusted With Power': AI Is COVID 2.0

Authored by J.B. Shurk via American Thinker,

We are living through some crazy times, aren't we? We oscillate between good and bad news so quickly that it feels as if we can't ever just relax and take a breath.

Perhaps that is the point. Perhaps the institutions that craft public "narratives" all day long have a vested interest in driving us insane. Surely an insane society is easier to control than a sane one if for no other reason than a confused population has no idea what to do next.

In conventional warfare, decoys and distractions draw an enemy's attention in one direction while the real action takes place somewhere else.

Information warfare operates the same way. Whatever is being discussed on cable news is almost always a smokescreen for something unfolding far away from news cameras.

items.content_text:
SAP Prepares To Cut 10,000 Jobs In Second Round Of AI Restructuring

German enterprise-software company SAP SE is preparing to cut at least 10,000 workers as part of a broader effort to reshape its operations, reduce costs, and improve efficiency through AI.

Bloomberg reported Thursday that the proposed cuts would affect at least 9% of SAP's global workforce of more than 110,000 employees. 

All departments have been asked to identify potential cuts, with product development, engineering, and sales set to see the most. The overhaul would also reshape how SAP builds and sells software as CEO Christian Klein accelerates its AI-first strategy.

More color from the report:

As part of the changes, SAP's leadership will continue to redesign how it develops and sells products, according to the people. Klein is seeking to embed AI tools into the company's applications, after earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems.

The proposed cuts would follow an AI-focused restructuring announced in 2024 and completed in early 2025 that slashed 10,000 positions and cost about 3.2 billion euros, largely through voluntary departures and internal retraining.

SAP's latest overhaul would add to a growing list of companies across Western countries using AI to restructure workforces and drive efficiencies.

Full list here.

On Wednesday, we highlighted a RAND report examining the fiscal consequences if AI displaces an estimated 10% to 15% of Americans' working hours over the next 15 years. The exposure extends to lawyers, analysts, software developers, and finance professionals, whose earnings generate a substantial share of income tax revenue. 

If AI squeezes those paychecks, what happens to the tax base supporting the federal government already running a $2 trillion deficit?

You'll Never Believe What 'Uranium One' Hillary Clinton Said About Nvidia Scandal

Hillary Clinton wants Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang called "Supergate."

"Is it a national security scandal? Yes," Clinton wrote on X on Monday, hours after Nvidia's board put Huang back in charge at President Trump's urging. "Is it a corruption scandal? Yes. Is it an insider trading scandal? Yes. Is it a market manipulation scandal? Yes."

Is it a national security scandal? Yes. 

Is it a corruption scandal? Yes. 

Is it an insider trading scandal? Yes. 

Is it a market manipulation scandal? Yes. 

If it's "super intelligence," call it Supergate.

— Hillary Clinton (@HillaryClinton) November 23, 2026

Of course - Clinton is uniquely qualified to spot a national-security and corruption scandal. As Secretary of State she sat on the CFIUS panel that approved the sale of Uranium One - owner of roughly 20% of US uranium production capacity - to Rosatom, Russia's state atomic-energy company. In the same period the Clinton Foundation and related entities took millions from Uranium One investors and other parties with a stake in the deal; Bill Clinton separately collected a $500,000 speaking fee from a Russian bank. The arrangement has never been fully investigated. She has also never been charged for the private server that, according to the FBI, handled 110 emails in 52 chains containing classified information, eight of those chains Top Secret. The same pattern appears in the Clinton Foundation's foreign-government donations while she ran the State Department and in the cattle-futures windfall that turned $1,000 into nearly $100,000 under the guidance of a Tyson Foods lawyer. None of it has stopped her from labeling the Nvidia board's decision a national-security, corruption, insider-trading, and market-manipulation scandal.

Piers Morgan read the post out on Wednesday's Piers Morgan Uncensored, introducing Clinton as someone "who knows a thing or two about scandals," and then laid out the case the newly elected Democrats will bring when they arrive in Washington in January. "An adulterous billionaire tech boss might have allowed a Chinese spying mistress to hand China an edge in the existential AI race," Morgan said. "They're going to have a field day. And frankly, it would be gross negligence if they didn't."

The spy half of that case has wobbled since the Wall Street Journal reported late Monday that US intelligence has no smoking gun on Alice Huang and that her links to Chinese intelligence may be only circumstantial, three weeks after the paper reported that officials in the US, Singapore and Taiwan feared she was a Chinese intelligence source.

Morgan then played Fox News host Jesse Watters, who sees it ending the same way. "The Democrats will likely use this scandal to impeach," Watters said. "They will say the president is manipulating the market to enrich himself and his cabinet." He added: "And a bunch of Republicans in Congress aren't going to defend him. So this is going to get ugly fast."

In the release announcing Huang's return, the board said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and, based on that input, is "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," according to the company's 8-K. "So in a nutshell, the president and his team told us there is nothing to see here," Morgan said.

Clinton knows the first charge on her list from the other side. In July 2016 the FBI concluded that she and her aides had been "extremely careless in their handling of very sensitive, highly classified information" on the private email server she used as secretary of state: 110 emails in 52 chains held information that was classified when sent or received, eight of the chains at Top Secret. Then-Director James Comey recommended no charges.

Clinton herself turned $1,000 into nearly $100,000 trading cattle futures in 1978 and 1979, guided by James Blair, a friend and a top lawyer for Tyson Foods, while her husband went from Arkansas attorney general to governor. The White House put her net gain at $26,521 for 1978 and $72,996 for 1979 when the trades came out in 1994. She was never charged.

None of that kept Joe Biden from awarding her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in January 2025. Now she is calling Trump's Nvidia rescue an insider trading scandal.

items.title: Georgia Voters To Decide Fate Of Massive $17 Billion Data Center After Furious Residents Revolt
items.content_text:
Georgia Voters To Decide Fate Of Massive $17 Billion Data Center After Furious Residents Revolt

Coweta County voters will decide in a Jan. 12 special election whether to repeal the rezoning for Project Sail, a $17 billion data center campus on more than 800 rural acres about 45 miles southwest of Atlanta that county commissioners approved 3-2 in April.

Probate Judge Carrie B. Markham ordered the election Monday. Opponents filed their petition Oct. 16 under the Home Rule provision of the Georgia Constitution, which let them force a vote with signatures from 10% of the county's electorate: 10,971 names, out of 109,703 active electors in the last general election, according to Markham's Nov. 23 order. Organizers turned in 14,820 signatures, and the county's director of elections verified 11,065 of them, clearing the bar by 94.

The ballot question reaches well past one project: besides repealing the April 7 rezoning, it would strip data centers from the county's zoning code and ban data centers and cryptocurrency mining operations in every zoning district in Coweta County. The order puts it to voters this way:

"Shall the action of the Coweta County Board of Commissioners on April 7, 2026 approving REZONE 24-019 be repealed, and Appendix A. Zoning and Development of the Coweta County Code of Ordinances be amended to delete data centers and data center campuses as permitted and conditional uses in all zoning districts and to prohibit data centers, data center campuses, cryptocurrency data centers, and cryptocurrency mining operations in all zoning districts of Coweta County?"

Atlas Development, the Buford-based company that filed the rezoning, objected to the petition on Oct. 23. Markham threw the objection out in a separate order the same day she called the election, finding that under Georgia Supreme Court precedent no party has legal standing to object to a petition filed under the Home Rule provision, and that Atlas's objection wasn't verified in any case.

The state's high court opened that door last year in a fight over Hogg Hummock, the Gullah Geechee community on Sapelo Island, when it ruled unanimously that a McIntosh County zoning ordinance was subject to the same referendum procedure Coweta's opponents used.

"The County became aware of this news at the same time as our citizens," Coweta's communications manager, Cathy Wickey, said in a statement. "Given the unique nature of this situation, we are still assessing its potential implications. We anticipate that legal questions and challenges may arise among the entities involved." The county will pay for the election, run it on its normal equipment and precincts, and the court will certify the result, according to the order.

Prologis, the San Francisco-based industrial REIT under contract to take over the project, said in October, when the petition's signatures came in, that the petition "does not change our commitment to Project Sail." Its executive JC Witt said in April that the site was chosen partly for its closeness to Georgia Power's Plant Yates, and that "the question isn't if this site will be developed. It's just how."

Atlas's filings with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs describe 13 buildings of about 378,000 square feet each, plus substations, finished by the end of 2036 and worth $17,161,900,000 at build-out. The same filings put its water demand at 9.1 million gallons a day, with 3.03 million gallons a day of sewage and 800 tons of solid waste a year. Prologis has pitched a smaller version, nine buildings and about 4.3 million square feet drawing roughly 900 megawatts.

The tax windfall that sold the project has shrunk: Atlas first projected more than $1 billion a year in local taxes, a figure the Atlanta Journal-Constitution found was erroneous; Prologis's latest projection is about $100 million a year, while the state filings list $163 million.

Commissioners Alphonso Smith, Jeff Fisher and John Reidelbach voted for the rezoning, which moved about 829 acres near Sargent and Wagers Mill roads from Rural Conservation to Industrial. "This is a no-brainer for the county," Smith said at the time. A group of residents sued in May in Coweta County Superior Court to void it, alleging that commissioners ignored the land's conservation designation and its role in groundwater recharge; that case is pending.

Yard signs against the project line home after home along Wagers Mill Road in Newnan. "The voters should have the right to decide," resident Leroy Kenner told Atlanta News First.

"We are thrilled with the Judge's order," Vivian Allen, a volunteer with Citizens for Rural Coweta, said in a release. "Thousands of our neighbors signed because they wanted a say, and we can't wait to see Coweta County turn out on January 12." Fellow volunteer Donna Boles credited the canvassers: "This happened because people stood in parking lots, on sidewalks, and at local events collecting signatures in the summer heat. This vote belongs to them."

Coweta has been on the front line of Georgia's data center build-out for months: Georgia Power is seizing homes and easements across Coweta and Fayette counties for a 35-mile, 500-kilovolt line to feed AI data centers. And when voters elsewhere got a direct say this month, 41 local measures in ten states went almost unanimously against the data centers.

If Coweta's measure passes on Jan. 12, it won't stop at Project Sail: no data center or crypto mine could be zoned anywhere in the county.
